Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 193, to amend the Act respecting the National Battlefields at Quebec. He said:
By this measure, the number of commissioners is increased from five to seven, and power is given to the commission to adopt by-laws for the administration of its affairs. The commission is further empowered to purchase, without the approval of the Governor in Council, any lands which it may have been authorized previously by Parliament to acquire, provided that funds have been appropriated for the purpose and are at the disposal of the commission.

Those are the three changes provided for in the amending Bill.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This appears to be a Bill which requires to be introduced byresolution. Section 11 says:
No expenditure shall be made and no liabilities shall be incurred by the commission until funds sufficient to cover such expenditure or liabilities shall be at its disposal for the purposes of this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was advisedthatitwas not necessary to precede this Bill by a resolution, but I shall bow to your judgment in the matter. No expenditure is contemplated by the Bill unless it has been provided for by Parliament. Under the existing legislation the commission may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, purchase lands provided it has been previously authorized by Parliament to acquire such lands. The purpose of this amending Bill is to prevent the delay which arises in the purchase of land, and which in the past has resulted disadvantageous^ to the commission in purchasing lands. The object of the provision which Your Honour has under consideration is to enable the commission, without obtaining the approval of the Governor in Council, to purchase properties, provided that the acquisition of such properties has been authorized by Parliament, and provided also that moneys for the purpose have been appropriated and are at the disposal of the commission. If Your Honour has any doubt as to the matter upon further consideration, I shall of course be glad to defer to your judgment and proceed by way of resolution; but I had been advised that it was not necessary in this case.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
On looking over the
section more carefully, I think perhaps the hon. gentleman is right. It says:
No expenditure shall be made and no liabilities shall be incurred by Jiie commission until funds sufficient to cover such expenditure or liabilities shall be at its disposal for the purposes of this Act.
If it were necessary to move by way of resolution, it would be only on this one section of the amending Bill. I will look into the mattter and find out what is the correct procedure.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Solicitor General) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 194, respecting Co-operative Credit Societies. He said:
No lengthy explanation will be necessary as the same Bill, with the exception of a few amendments, was introduced by myself last session. Furthermore, last session I had the honour of addressing the House upon the question at large. My remarks upon that occasion will apply to the present Bill, and I will explain it more fully on the second reading. This Bill provides for uniform machinery throughout the Dominion enabling the formation of cooperative credit societies. I do not need to describe the character of the societies for which co-operative credit is provided. They are societies, the principle of which ia mutual loanings among its members of funds for the purpose of their commercial advantage. Certain restrictions are placed upon each society, and the general precautions provided under the previous Bill are embodied here. I may add that the Bill does not differ in any essential particular from that passed by this House, after a very thorough review in Committee, in 1907.
Is it the intention of my hon. friend to press this Bill during the present session?

That is my intention
and my hope. I do not think it will entail the sacrifice of a great deal of the time of the ,House, because the attention of the House has already been given to the principle, and, in large .measure, to the details. Consequently, I do not think I am asking a great deal of the House in asking that this Bill should pass.
Is it the intention to restrict the districts in which these companies work, or is permission to be given them to circulate all over the country?
It is Dominion-wide.

The previous Bill was
passed by the House but rejected by the Senate. Is it the same Bill exactly or does it differ in some respects?

That is the Bill to which I referred in my opening remarks. The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) was chairman of the committee on that Bill, and that committee reviewed the measure in great detail. This Bill differs from that in some respects, but in principle it is the same. Any changes that have been made are dictated by the experience of banks that have been organized since that Bill was before the House.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

[u'The Solicitor General has bailed out $58,000,000, and he has brought it down to $100,000,000. What does that mean? That -is Mackenzie and Mann's price as promoters for carrying on this work, acting as financial agents, acting as constructive agents. That is their price for their services for all these years' work.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not want you to get the idea that I think Mackenzie and Mann should not be allowed something. I certainly think they should. They are farsighted, energetic, earnest men and they should get reasonable recognition, but I say that $60,000,000 of stock which the Solicitor General says some day will foe worth dollar for dollar is too much money for Canada to pay to two men for promoting a transcontinental railway in this country. Not only is it too much for these men to get, but it is too much for Canada to pay freight rates on. Who is going to pay these freight rates ? Again it has to come out of the West, not only on that $60,000,000, but on that $40,000,000 that Canada has taken as her share, if I might use the term, of "the booty. Freight rates have to be paid on that. It is not like a royalty in a mine. When you take a royalty on a mineral, you take a product which is easily worked. The intrinsic value is there. It is not in the working that the value exists; the . value exists because somebody is fortunate in finding the mineral and there is a huge profit; but in this case, this road on that $100,000,000 has to earn $6,000,000 annually which has to be taken out of the pockets of the people in rates, and it means that the cost of living in the West will be that much higher. What will be the argument of my good friend Mr. Phippen before the Eailway Commission the next time that freight rates are being discussed ? He is going to say this: In the determination of these rates, you have to take into consideration this $100,000,000. Canada through her Parliament recognizes that that is a fair amount to pay these men for their services. Canada has taken $40,000,000 of it in return for her guarantee; and we represent the Canadian Northern, and Mackenzie and Mann demand that you fix the freight rates at such an amount that there will be a fair return on the money which you must
consider as capital invested. That is the policy which the Government has asked me to commit myself to, but I am not prepared to do so. The great broad principle is the principle of a partnership. You, Mr. Speaker, may say: The hon. member has no experience; he is young in Parliament so far; he was prejudiced against these men; they have struck at him and he has struck back; he is hurt. But let me establish my case in the light of history, and it is only in the experience of the past that you can reach the conclusions as to what should be done in the present and as to what will happen in the future. This is not the first time that Canada has experimented in railroad partnerships. In 1852, Upper Canada began to pay the price when she entered into a partnership with the Grand Trunk Eailway Company. By the terms of that arrangement Canada was to have nine directors and the Grand Trunk were to have nine, and what was said at the time? . The inspector general, Mr. Hincks, spoke in severe terms of the misrepresentations made by the enemies of this undertaking respecting the effect which it was said to have on the credit of the province. He denied altogether that the Government was interested in the slightest degree in the cost of the undertaking, whatever it might be. The province paid nothing; it would only promise to guarantee the amount of \xa33,000 per mile, for which it was to have the first mortgage on the road with interest at .six per cent. He did not care how much the stockholders laid out on the road; the more they expended the better . it was for the province. One thing he was pretty certain of, the Grand Trunk Eailway Company would not ask for a single penny from the province, for they could get money in England at a much less rate than six per cent without being subject to the restrictions which were to be imposed upon them if they accepted the Government guarantee, in having directors on the part of the province.
In 1854, the Grand Trunk Eailway Company came back again to the Government of the day in Upper Canada. In 1855, they came back again. In 1856, they came' back again and they asked to be allowed to issue preferential bonds to the extent of \xa32,000,000. In 1857 the Government were so disgusted with the whole thing that what did they do? They brought in a measure to sever the connection between the executive and the commercial enterprise. Listen to what Mr. Cayley said in 1857. He was then inspector', "general which is practicaly Minister of Finance:
The first object of this Bill is to dispense with the Government directors in the company. The position of Government directors has been the occasion of casting upon the Government a good deal of reflection. All the management on the part of the Grand Trunk Railway Company has been cast upon or attempted to be cast upon the Government. The position has been an unenviable one. Now we propose to do away with the responsibility of the Government, and to give the entire management into the hands of the company. It has been suggested one member of the Government in tre board with a view of exercising a supervision over its affairs, but this arrangement in the board with a view of exercising only leave to that member the same responsibility while depriving him of the advice and support of his colleagues.
In the light of the experience of Upper Canada, in the light of the economic conditions 'that I have laid before this House to-night, the Government ask me to support this measure. All I have to say is that I' cannot see eye to eye with them. I have tried to place fairly before the House my reasons ior my stand. If they are incorrect, it is open to other gentlemen to refute them; 'but as I have spoken, so I believe.

I received a letter this morning which informs me that Mr. Briegel, superintendent of the railway mail service in Montreal, an old gentleman who has rendered faithful service to His Majesty for over forty years, is about to retire upon pension and that the department contemplates appointing as his successor Mr. W. L. Cark-ner, of Quebec city. Mr. Carkner has been in the service for two years only and has never passed the examinations which are required of the other officers. I do not know him personally and he may be a good public servant, but I would call the attention of the Postmaster General to the fact that there are in the post office department at Montreal other gentlemen, friends of his, who have been in the service a very long time and Who should be entitled to promotion. I might name, for instance, Messrs. Methot, Villeneuve and Forest. If the staff in the Montreal post office is not to be demoralized-my hon friend appreciates the sense in which I use the word-the principle of filling vacancies >by promotion should be recognized. The railway mail service is a complicated service, and the man who is at its head should be fully equipped for his duties and fully cognizant of the conditions that exist all over the immense district of Montreal. I do not think it would be fair
to the staff or in the interests of the service that a new man should be brought from another district and given this position in Montreal. Personally I know nothing about the facts, but I am informed that the hon. minister was approached on the subject, that he gave his decision in . favour of Mr. Carkner and that the appointment is about to be made. I would like the hon minister to state whether or not this is the case, and whether or not he will follow the good old golden rule of filling vacancies by promotion, especially in a branch of the service which is certainly one of the most important.

Mr. Briegel, who has been connected with the department for a very long time, has given most devoted and efficient service. If he is not quite as capable of working now as he was some years ago, on account of old age, his services are still very valuable to the department, and I shall certainly not ask him to resign or to be pensioned. If the time comes-and I hope it will not be in the near future- when he cannot accomplish his work in an efficient way, he will understand without anybody telling him what he should do.
I am happy to say that that time has not yet come, and so far as I am concerned, I have had no requests from Mr. Briegel to be pensioned; my officers inform me that they also have received no such request. I certainly shall not touch upon the question of his successor until such request is received, for I would not do anything which would hurt Mr. Briegel's feelings.

So far as Mr. Briegel is concerned, that is quite satisfactory. I agree with my hon. friend that Mr. Briegel is an old and faithful servant and that he is quite capable of fulfilling his duties for many months, and, I hope, for many years to come. The hon. member for St.Lawrence is aware that Mr. Briegel is universally known in Montreal, and that he is very popular with the public on account of his courtesy and devotion to duty. It would be a thousand pities if he were removed and pensioned when he is still able to render valuable service to the department. I may say frankly to the hon. minister that the gentleman who informed me in the matter says that the minister was lately approached with regard to Mr. Briegel's successor, and that the hon. gentleman said that Mr. Carkner would be appointed immediately after the close of the session. I am glad, however, to take the word of the hon. Postmaster General that nothing of

the kind will happen. I have the highest regard for my Quebec friends, but surely there are enough public servants in the post office at Montreal able to succeed Mr. Briegel without importing one from another district. It that were done it would cause a great deal of feeling.

It would be absolutely improper on my part to discuss the successor of Mr. Briegel when he is in charge of the office, and I intend that he shall stay in charge so long as he desires and so long as his services are efficient.
Hear, hear.

I have not said to
anybody that this matter was settled. I think it would have been indelicate on my part to do any such thing without having first heard from Mr. Briegel. So there is nothing decided, nothing settled. As to the question of bringing an officer from Quebec to Montreal or from Montreal to Quebec, I would not hesitate for a moment to do that if I thought it would be in the interest of the service. We have sent people from the East to the West and vice versa, and I believe that my hon. friend did the same thing. We are having some complaint about that in the West, but we [DOT]consider the Post Office Department to be, to a certain extent, in the position of a bank which has branches all over the country. A bank will move its employees or clerks from office to office for the proper carrying out of its business and the efficiency of its service. While we are always prepared to give promotions to the employees of a branch in their own town, when any circumstances require that we move one employee from one district to another we shall certainly do so without being estopped by .the question o'f the place where he formerly lived. The gentleman to whom my hon. friend from Rouville referred is a very good employee in the railway mail branch in Montreal. I understand that he is a very efficient help to Mr. Briegel, but there are others too. In other words I have not looked into the question, and I shall not look into it or decide it so long as our good employee Mr. Briegel is in charge.
I have made inquiries about the other matter of which I spoke and I find that the two items in the supplementaries for the year ending March 31, 1914, had been left in the portfolio of the clerk. We might dispose of them now. There are accounts due which should be paid out of these items, but of course payment cannot now be made.
As these votes are in the Supplementary Estimates of the last fiscal year, I think the minister should inquire whether it will not be necessary for him to introduce a special Supply Bill.

I have taken the
opinion of the assistant Clerk o'f the House, who says that he has not the least doubt that we can pass the items now.
But after the items have passed, as the Supply Bill for 1914 has gone through, if will be necessary to put these in a separate schedule of the next Supply Bill and have that passed.
My hon. friend is quite right; that is what I am told.

A few days ago I placed a question on the Order Paper, which was answered by the Postmaster General. The question and answer are as follows:
Mr. Tobin:
1.	Has Mr. J. R. Denison, postmaster of Richmond, Quebec, been dismissed? If so, on what grounds?
2.	Was an investigation held? If so, by whom and did Mr. Denison have an opportunity of defending himself? If not, why not?
3.	Has a new postmaster been appointed? If so, what is his name and who recommended his appointment?
Mr. Pelletier:
1.	Tes. The management of the office was very unsatisfactory.
2.	Serious complaints were made in regard to the management of the office and an official investigation was held. The inspector's report showed that a change in the postmastership was necessary.
3.	A new postmaster has been appointed by the direction of the Postmaster General. His name is Wm. E. Mclver.
It seems that the Postmaster General has a kind of brutal way-
Order.

-of dismissing old employees. Mr. Denison, who has been postmaster bf Richmond for the past sixteen years, has, as far as I know, given satisfaction to the public; and up to April 22 last, I believe, he was not aware that any mistakes had [DOT]been made in his office. But on the 22nd of April last he received this letter from the inspector of the district:
To the Postmaster,
Richmond, Quebec.
Dear Sir,
I beg to notify you that I have received notice from the department at Ottawa that you have been dismissed from the postmastership of Richmond for unsatisfactory management. The transfer will take place as soon as arrangements can be made.

In answer to tliat letter, Mr. Denison *wrote to the inspector on the 23rd of April as follows:
L. E. Dastous, Esq.,
Post Office Inspector,
Sherbrooke, P.Q.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of yours of the 22nd inst., advising me that I have been dismissed from the postmastership of Richmond for unsatisfactory management.
I must say that this seems to me to he a very peculiar letter to have received, and I would ask you to register my protest against this, and to advise me wherein the unsatisfactory management has occurred. It seems to me that I should have been advised of any investigation which has been made into the working of this office, and to have had a chance to have put in my defence.
Will you please procure for me copies of any complaints which have been made against me, bv whom they were made, and also what steps were taken to investigate this matter.
J. R. Denison.
I am surprised, yet in another way I am not, at the stand taken by the Post Office Department. It seems they have no regard for justice at all when .they wish to distribute patronage. I quite understand that some weeks ago there was a tour through the Eastern Townships of certain members of this Government, and I have no dou'bt that one of the promises they *made at Richmond was that Mr. Denison's head should be cut off to make room for one of their own friends; but why did they not dismiss him in the proper way? Why did they not hold an investigation and give the accused a chance .to defend himself? If that had been done I should have had nothing to say, but, as it was, the man was dismissed without any investigation, and I would ask the Postmaster General why that investigation was not held? Mr. Denison would like to have the satisfaction of- knowing what he was dismissed for.

I am somewhat surprised to hear the hon. member for Richmond and Wolfe raising this question in the way he has done. Politics do not enter into this case at all. I want to tell my hon. friend at once that the Hon. Mr. Per-ley has not in any way been the cause of the dismissal of this postmaster. That question, to my knowledge, was never discussed at all during the visit which my two colleagues made in the Eastern Townships. I might say that for a long time previous to this dismissal it had been represented to .me that the postmaster at Richmond was not giving the public satisfaction. I made inquiries, and was told that
if I could leave this postmaster in charge it would be a good thing from some other point of view than the service, seeing that he was an old man; and I have kept him there for the last twelve or fifteen months. He was not accused of taking any part in politics, and that is not the reason for his dismissal. He has been dismissed purely from the point of view of efficiency in
12	noon, the transaction of the business of that post office- nothing more or less. My hon. frien'd says that an investigation should have been held. Let me tell my hon. friend that I did not go into this matter blindly. This man was dismissed as the result of an investigation. I am sure we have a report in the department from our officials notifying me that the business of the post office at Richmond was not transacted in a satisfactory manner to the public, and that a change should consequently be made. I have not the report before me, as I was not informed that this matter was going to be brought up, when I asked my friends opposite to let me know what matters they were going to 'deal with so that I might have the papers. My hon. friend has chosen to use the word ' brutal ' in referring to this man's dismissal. I did not rise to a point of order at that word because I did not think the hon. member for Richmond and Wolfe, whom everybody knows is a very good fellow, really meant what is implied by that word. There was no brutality about it at all. The postmaster in question has been kept on for a long time, in spite of representations made to me that the business of that post office was not carried out as it should be. Gradually the representations became more pressing, but I said that I would not dismiss the man until the regular and proper investigation had been held. That investigation took place, and the report showed that there was nothing else for me to do but to replace this man in order to give efficient and satisfactory service to the public. Under the circumstances, I do not think the remarks of my hon. friend are just and fair to me.

Does the Postmaster General think it is right to 'dismiss this man after he has served the public for sixteen years? The Postmaster General admits that no complaints have been made as to Mr. Denison's interfering in politics. Mr. Denison is a Liberal, but he has never interfered in politics one way or the other. He is an honourable gentleman, who is

respected throughout the whole district; and I would ask the Postmaster General if he thinks it fair that Mr. Denison should receive such a letter of dismissal from the post office inspector without any other notice having been given? For the information of the Postmaster General and the House, I will read the letter once more:
The Postmaster,
Richmond, Que.
Dear Sir,-I beg to notify you that I have received notice from the department at Ottawa that you have been dismissed from the postmastership of Richmond, for unsatisfactory management.
The transfer will take place as soon as arrangements can be made.
Yours truly,
(Signed) L. E. Dastous,
Post Office Inspector.
The Postmaster General objects to my using the word ' brutal.' But is that word too strong, considering how this old servant has been treated? This man wrote to the post office inspector on the 23rd of April asking for an investigation, and a chance to defend himself. Was it unreasonable of him to expect British fair play at the hands of the Postmaster General? He was accused of mismanagement of the business of his post office, and he should not have been held guilty until the charge had been proved. But the Post Office Department does not want any light thrown on their investigations; they hold their investigations in the Eastern Townships in a dark room. Mr. Denison was not given a chance to defend himself. I am sure he is not looking for the small salary attached to that post office. He is a wealthy man, well able to provide for himself, but he objects to being dismissed in this way. I will ask the Postmaster General a direct question: Does he approve of that letter of dismissal that the post office inspector sent to Mr. Denison on the 22nd April?

The post office inspector having received instructions from the Post Office Department to change the postmaster at Richmond had nothing else to do but notify Mr. Denison of his dismissal, and I cannot blame the inspector for doing what was his duty. My hon. friend seems to be under a misapprehension as to the facts. I told him a moment ago that I was not aware of any charge of partisanship having been made against this man. We have our regular officers whose duty it is to look into these cases of improper management of a post office, and who report to the department whether the 
office is being properly managed or not. In this case the regular course has been followed. We have a report which says that the management of the office was such that an investigation was held and that the change in the postmastership was desirable.
On what grounds?

Had my hon. friend
given me notice I would have brought the papers. I cannot remember the exact tenor of the report but I am almost sure I gave instructions to name another postmaster because of the report of the officials which justified that course. If I remember aright the report of the officer was such that I would not have done my duty had I kept that postmaster there. I am sorry to have to go so far in my statement, but it is the fault of the hon. member (Mr. Tobin) and not mine. I do not know the postmaster, I never saw him, but will the hon. gentleman say that when I have a report from the officers of the department telling me a change must take place on account of mismanagement, that I should refuse to act on that report?

I did not give the Postmaster General' notice in the House, but last evening after the House adjourned I told him that it was my intention to take the matter up. I am pleased to hear the Postmaster General say there are no politics in this, but I know the contrary, and the supporters of the Government in the Eastern Townships know it also. The minister without portfolio and the Secretary of State could not stop off there during their visit but they had Mr. Baker. I do not know what you call him; I call him their sleight-of-hand man, that is the member for Brome; he stopped off there. Perhaps he expects to step into the gap some day and become a minister. The secretary of the minister without portfolio stopped off there also to settle some questions -as to a site for a post office. When the Postmaster General gets the report of these gentlemen he will discover that his friends down there were not throwing bouquets at each other. Did the Postmaster General inform Mr. Denison that this investigation would be held?

The investigation was held by the official of the department who was instructed to do so, and I cannot say whether notice was given or not. I feel

sure that the usual and proper course was taken. In what particular does Mr. Denison claim that he had no notice? Let me read the following letter from Mr. Denison to the post office inspector:
Richmond, P.Q., April 23, 1914. L. E. Dastous, Esq.,

Sherbrooke, P.Q.
Dear Sir:-
I beg to acknowledge receipt of yours of the 22nd instant, advising me that I have been dismissed from the postmastership of Richmond, for unsatisfactory management.

It seems to me that I should have been advised of any investigation which has been made into the working of this office, and to have had a chance to put in my defence.
Will you please procure for me, copies of any complaint which have been made against me, and by whom they were made, and also what steps were taken to investigate this matter.
Mr. Denison wrote me yesterday that he had not got any answer to that letter. I beg also to read the following letter from Mr. Denison:
I might say that about the 10th day of March, 1914, Mr. Dastous, the post office inspector, came to Richmond, and stated that he had a complaint and charge to lay against me, in connection with the office. J. Ewing, J.P., administered the oath to her. That is the only notice the postmaster had of what the Postmaster General calls an investigation. I do not wish to take up any more time in the matter, but I think I can ask the Postmaster General to investigate this case more fully, because the
people of the Eastern townships, and especially the people of Richmond and Wolfe, have been treated very harshly by his department in the last two or three years. He is out of the game.

The department
thought fit, from the point of view of business, to establish a branch of our inspection office in the city of Sherbrooke for the Eastern Townships. That existed years ago and was abolished. Believing they were entitled to it, I gave it back to them, and I am proud -of having done so.

And you call it
business to act on that ground?
Yes.
Then the post office inspection office is a matter of political patronage and favour, and not a matter of business.
Not at all.
That is what you said.
I say the Eastern Townships were entitled to that office.

The public interest.
Explain that.
I took it for granted that my hon. friends would have guessed that, but, seeing that their minds are so far away from the public interest, I now state it.
What about the" reason the hon. gentleman gave a moment ago-that the office had been taken away, and they had the right to have it restored.
These statements do not clash at all. The office had been established, and then it was abolished.
Why?
For some political reason.
To cut down expenses.

It was necessary that it should be re-opened, because the business in the Montreal office was so great that it could not be taken care of properly. So we re-established that office. And we have established another one at Joliette.
One at Joliette?
Yes, a branch. And 1 am re-instating the one at Three Rivers.
Hear, hear.
I thought that would please my hon. friend.
It does not.
When was this done?
We are doing it now. The amount was voted last session. The office at Joliette will be a branch of the Montreal office.

But Sherbrooke is by
itself?
But not inspection branches, there is only one inspection head office.
No, they have district inspectors.
But the Montreal bank eastern inspection district includes the Maritime provinces and Newfoundland.

How is it that we hear so much about this now, when this vote was passed last session? My hon. friend from Richmond and Wolfe and my hon. friend from Sherbrooke were both members of the House then. Why did not'they raise their voices against it?
If we are to criticise all that comes before us the session will last the whole year.

But it takes no more time to criticise it in advance than to criticise it afterwards. When it was proposed that money should be voted for this purpose there was unanimous consent, anl now complaint is made about it. The hon. member complains of the number of employees there. There are five, if I am not mistaken. I think that one of these was in the post office at Sherbrooke before. There is another, Mr. Soles, to whom the hon. member refers. This gentleman was taken from the Montreal office on account of his experience and knowledge of the business of the inspector's office and transferred to Sherbrooke.
He belongs to the eastern townships.

He originally came
from there. He wag a pretty good officer in Montreal, and when the office in Sherbrooke was re-opened, we had to have a man there with experience, so we asked Mr. Soles to go to the Sherbrooke office. He consented, and he is paid for his Sherbrooke work as he would have been paid for his Montreal work.
Mr. Dastous was appointed in Sherbrooke ?
Yes.
Has he had any experience ?

For a certain length of time-I would not care to state the exact number of months-Mr. Dastous worked in Quebec under the instructions of the Quebec post office inspector in order to learn what had to be learned about the duties of an inspector. That is a businesslike way, I should think, of administering the depart-
[Mr. A. K. Maclean.!
ment. The other man, Mr. Soles, who was sent from Montreal, has had considerable experience, and we are satisfied that we now have in Sherbrooke an office which is a credit to the Eastern Townships, anid which should not be criticised as it is to-day by hon. gentlemen opposite.
If I remember rightly, the Post Office Act requires that no one shall be appointed superintendent unless he has had a certain number of years' experience.
That does not apply to inspectors.
Was Mr. Dastous employed by the department before he was made inspector ? I always thought that he was a dealer in flour and grain in Sherbrooke.

How far west do the Sherbrooke and Three Rivers inspection divisions extend ?
I will get the information for my hon. friend and give it to him this afternoon or to-morrow morning.
Does the Sherbrooke inspection division extend to St. Lambert or St. Johns ?

I should think that
would be in the Montreal district. I will get the information.

May I ask the minister to give similar information as to the territory covered by the office to be opened at Three Rivers. Has the minister in view the person who is to be appointed as inspector ? If not, I might submit a name.
An assistant inspector is to be appointed at Three Rivers. It is to toe a branch of the inspector's office.
Under the control of the Montreal or of the Quebec inspector?
Quebec.
Has the hon. Postmaster General received applications for the position?
A very great number.
Would the hon. minister explain the difference between the two amounts given in answer to the same question asked on different occasions by the hon. member for Sherbrooke?

One explanation would be that the salary of Mr. Soles, which is, I understand, $2,000, is not a new expenditure; it is paid at Sherbrooke instead o'f at Montreal. However, I will look into that and give my hon. friend the information.

Before the hon. Postmaster General leaves the question of the Sherbrooke post office I think it my duty to resent the insinuation which he has just made against the Eastern Townships' members. In the course of a very aible speech he insinuated that the hon. members from the Eastern Townships, including the hon. member for Sherbrooke, who is not in his seat, and myself, are opposed to the opening of an inspection office at Sherbrooke. I never said a word in this House in opposition to the opening of an inspection office in Sherbrooke; I do not think the hon. member for Sherbrooke ever said a word in this House against the opening of that office, and I fail to understand from anything which has been said by the hon. member for Richmond and Wolfe to-day that he is opposed to the opening of that office. The hon. Postmaster General, who continually rises in his place and tells hon. gentlemen on this side that they ought to be fair, should himself treat the members of the Opposition fairly and not put in their mouths words that they never uttered or make any such insinuations as he has made on this occasion.
I made no insinuations whatever. What is the tenor of the discussion which has been taking place in this committee?

The tenor of the discussion in this committee is whether or not the Post Office Department is run on a businesslike basis. The hon. member for Richmond and Wolfe was proving that it was not run on a businesslike basis, because two answers to the same question, given within fifteen days of each other, showed a difference of $4,000. The hon. member for Richmond and Wolfe said that that is not businesslike; there is no objection whatever to the opening of an inspection office at Sherbrooke.

When I said that this should not be criticised because it was passed by the House last session, the hon. membeT for Beauce said: we have no time to criticise everything and it would take twelve months to do that.

That is because you
bring these matters up at the end of the session.

Whether at the end of the session or not, if it is wrong, I should be told that it is wrong; if it is passed unanimously, I take it for granted that everybody agrees. This discussion will be understood by the people as meaning that the expenditure which we are making in Sherbrooke for this inspection office is a useless expenditure and should not be made. I want there to be no misapprehension about this matter. Let us take it for granted that the hon. member for Shefford voices the sentiments of hon. members from the Eastern Townships. I give him credit for what he has said and I accept his word, but let it be well understood that all the hon. members from the Eastern Townships approve the opening of the inspection office at Sherbrooke.
Run on a business basis.
Very good; what was wrong a moment ago is all right now.

That is not fair, Mr. Chairman. The hon. Postmaster General has the knack of making assertions that are not always exactly correct. He says that the public will be under the impression, from the discussion that has taken place here, that the expenditure which is proposed to be made in the Eastern Townships is useless. We may criticise the expenditure, but we may, nevertheless, approve the establishment of an inspection office in the Eastern Townships. We may criticise part of the expenditure, and we may admit that another part of it is all right, and it is not fair that the Postmaster General should come here and say: as a whole, you are opposed to the principle of this thing, and you must not criticise. My hon. friend asks us why we did not criticise last year. We had nothing to criticise. He was asking for an expenditure of money, and we thought that that money would be expended in the businesslike manner which he boasts of as being characteristic of the administration of his department. for Richmond or any other member could not criticise this item before the information was available, and it is not right that the Postmaster General should endeavour to convey the impression that hon. members of the Opposition oppose the establishment of an inspection office when they do not oppose it. oppose this expenditure. We do not know how the money is going to be expended and I claim that the criticism made by the hon. member for Richmond is a proper one. If my hon. friend
would excuse me, I think it would be only fair to the hon. member for Richmond if I gave the information for which he asked.

remarks made by the Postmaster General. Was there anything in my remarks that was against the opening of inspection offices in the district of St. Francois ? I do not say that the office is good or bad. We have not opposed it in any way. Why was my friend compelled to open the office? He knows and the people in the Eastern Townships and Sherbrooke know that it is because a party in Sherbrooke held a pistol to his ear and said:	You have to do this and give
Mr. Dastous a position. The collector of customs, Mr. Stenson, an ex-member of this House, died. The French-Canadian people 
of Sherbrooke said that this position belonged to them, but the Minister of Customs gave it to an English-speaking gentleman. a good Conservative and a young man whom I respect. I am coming to that
now. My hon. friend will see that all the fuss he has made about this does not amount to much in the face of the facts.

I would advise my
hon. friend not to get excited. I am trying to give the facts. After I have given them, and if he has a reason, my hon. friend can become excited. Richmond, Que., Feb. 11, 1914. The Hon. the Postmaster General,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-As a citizen of the town of Richmond I hereby complain of the management of the post office at Richmond.
The present postmaster, J. R. Denison, never had the education or business training required for the management of such an office-
I know all about it.

The letter goes on:
__and as he is now upwards of 80 years of
age and very deaf, is utterly unable to render the public efficient service, nor does he engage employees capable of doing the work for him.

The postmaster and his assistants do not sort the mail properly. Almost daily, I receive other people's letters in my box, and I find that letters addressed to me have been given to others, always causing serious delay in receiving them ; and I have reason to believe that sometimes I have never received them. I have heard the same complaints from all the other business men and the townspeople generally.
Persons not employees of the post office (even children) are allowed to enter the office, pick out their own mail before it is sorted and also assist in the general distribution. As a large mail receiver X find these conditions intolerable, and make this complaint hoping that a competent person will be sent to investigate the truth of the facts alleged.
In addition to sending this complaint myself, it is my intention to show it to a few of the business men of the town more particularly interested in the conduct of the postmaster, and to ask them also to sign this if they can bear out my statements and approve of the complaint.
Yours very truly,
Charles Campbell.
The complaint is signed by five other people: John Hayes, M.D.

The man that Tobin
licked.
The defeated candidate in 1911.

Who will come back next time. It is signed also by A. Rain-bach, George J. Alexander, Mr. W. H. Keenan and E. S. Bernard. I received this in February, long before Hon. Mr. Pea-ley went through the Eastern Townships. It was sent to Hon. Mr. Per ley, and he sent it to me. Whereas the Canadian Northern Railway Company hereinafter called the 'Canadian Northern' has represented that the several companies set forth in the first schedule to these resolutions, and their railways and undertakings, rolling stock, equipment, assets and properties are intended to constitute a transcontinental railway system to be denominated the 'Canadian Northern System' and that the Canadian Northern desires to control said system by the ownership or control of the shares or majorities thereof in the capital stock of the said companies, and that it now owns or controls the shares or majorities thereof in the capital stock of certain of the said companies, and that the several companies are desirous that aid should be granted for the purpose of completing the construction and equipment of﻿MAY 13, 1914
the works and undertakings of the Canadian Northern system and for the betterment thereof;
And whereas it is in the interest of Canada that the desired aid should be granted.
It is therefore resolved that it is expedient to provide as follows :-
1.	That His Majesty on behalf of the Dominion of Canada may aid the construction, completion, equipment and betterment of the Canadian Northern system by guaranteeing payment of the principal and interest of the bonds, debentures, debenture stock or other securities, hereinafter called the (guaranteed securities of the Canadian Northern, to an amount not exceeding forty-five million dollars ($45,000,000) which guaranteed securities, to the extent aforesaid, the Canadian Northern is hereby authorized to create and issue; interest on the guaranteed securities to be at the rate of four per cent per annum payable half-yearly, the principal to be payable not later than a day in the year 1934.
2.	That the guaranteed securities shall be secured by a trust deed, hereinafter called the 'New Trust Deed' made to a trustee or trustees approved by the Governor in Council, hereinafter called the 'Trustee' and the same shall in manner and terms satisfactory to the Governor in Council,-
(a)	Grant a first, fixed, and specific mortgage or charge upon the shares mentioned in the first part of the second schedule hereto;
<b) Grant a specific mortgage or charge upon the mortgage securities and shares of stock now or from time to time hereafter deposited with and specifically mortgaged under the Trust Deed of the 30th day of June, 1903, hereinafter called the 'Perpetual Consolidated Debenture Stock Trust Deed' those now so deposited and mortgaged being mentioned in the second part of the said Second Schedule;
(c)	Grant fixed, specific and floating mortgages or charges upon the undertaking of the Canadian Northern and its properties, assets, rents and revenues, and its rights, powers and franchises, present and future;
(d)	Grant a fixed and specific charge upon the equity of redemption of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, in $10,000,000 of capital stock and $10,000,000 of First Debenture Stock of the Canadian Northern Town Properties Company, Limited (the subsidiary company mentioned in the eighth clause of the trust deed dated the 19th of November, 1913, made between the Canadian Northern Railway Company, Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, The British Empire Trust Company, Limited, and the National Trust Company, Limited, trustees, securing £3,500,000 of five per cent Land Mortgage Debentures), the said capital stock and First Debenture Stock being now held by the said Trustees as part of the mortgaged premises under the said trust deed.
(2) The Mortgages and charges to be granted under (b) and (c) of this section shall be subject to and rank next after the mortgages and charges heretofore created and the securities heretofore or hereafter created or issued under the existing trust deeds or mortgages securing the same, and to the powers of issuing securities having priority therein reserved and contained.
3.	That before a guarantee is given the following conditions shall be complied with:
(a)	The agreement a draft whereof is set forth in the third schedule hereto, (hereinafter called the ' Agreement ' shall be duly executed
by the parties thereto, and the Governor in Council is hereby authorized to execute the same.
(b)	There shall be transferred to and vested in the Trustee as part of the mortgaged premises the shares of stock mentioned in subclause (a) of section 2 of these resolutions free from prior charges thereon, such shares to become and to remain the property of the Canadian Northern, subject to the charge created by and to the terms of the New Trust Deed. Provided that the necessary shares to qualify the directors and preserve the corporate entities of the respective companies may remain in the name of such directors and other necessary parties, but the share certificates ready for transfer shall be delivered to and held by or for the Trustee of the New Trust Deed.

(d)	There shall be transferred to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General of Canada in trust for the Government of Canada, three hundred and thirty thousand fully paid shares of the par value of $100 each of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern and such shares shall be the absolute property of His Majesty in right of the Dominion of Canada. The said shares or any part thereof may be disposed of under the authority of Parliament upon such terms and conditions as it may determine, and the proceeds of the sale thereof paid into the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada. Pending the disposal of the said shares and of the seventy thousand shares issued to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General of Canada, pursuant to section 8 of chapter 10 of the statutes of 1913, all voting and other rights under the said shares shall be exercisable by the said Minister of Finance and the Receiver General or by whomsoever he may from time to time appoint.

ment of payment thereof will he taken or pressed.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it is desirable that a brief statement of the situation, which confronts the country in connection with the Canadian Northern railway, and an explanation of the proposals which have been placed before the House, should be given before the House goes into Committee on this resolution.
The Canadian Northern railway had its beginning in 1896 in the construction of 100 miles of railway in the western part of the province of Manitoba, under the charter of a company known as the Lake Manitoba Railway and Canal Company. The enterprise of building this road had been undertaken in 1889, and those who sought to promote that enterprise had signally failed in their undertaking. Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann acquired the charter of the road and constructed it, and it was put into operation about 1896. Afterwards other roads from time to time were purchased, other charters were procured and additional mileage was constructed, so that the system at the present time extends into every province of Canada except, I think, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
The system has to-day in operation 7,236-51 miles; it has also under construction with track laid, but the road not in operation, 1,542-26 miles; it has grade completed, but no track yet laid, 850-52 miles; it has grade not completed but under contract, 230-08 miles; which gives a total of nearly 10,000 miles.
The status of the railway as a potential transcontinental railway was realized in Parliament, according to my recollection, as early as 1903 or 1904, and its status as such was definitely recognized in 1911 by chap. 6 of the statutes of that year. The following recital is to be found in that Act which provided for certain aid to the Canadian Northern Railway Company:
Whereas, having regard to the growth of population and the rapid development of the production and trade of that portion of Canada lying west of the Great Lakes, and to the rapidly expanding trade and commerce of Canada generally, it is in the interests of Canada as a whole that another line of railway designed to assist in the direct and economic interchange of traffic between the eastern and western portions of Canada, to open up and develop portions as yet without railway facilities, to promote the internal and foreign trade of Canada, to develop commerce through Canadian ports, and to afford the Government system of railways in Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island an interchange of through traffic, should be constructed from the Pacific Ocean to the city of Montreal: And whereas the projected line of the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company extending from Port Arthur to the city of Montreal will provide the uncompleted portion of the said through line lying north and east of the Great Lakes.
The statute last mentioned provided for a guarantee of bonds of the Canadian Northern railway from Montreal to Port Arthur, about 1,000 miles in length, to the amount of $35,000 per mile. By chapter 7 of the statutes of 1912 a guarantee of -bonds of the same amount in respect of 115 miles in the province of Alberta, to the boundary of British Columbia, was also authorized.
The aid which has been granted to the company, whether in lands or in subsidies, whether by the federal Government or by the provincial governments or by municipalities, is set out at pages 10 and 13 of the printed documents which are upon the table of the House and which have been dis-

tributed among hon. gentlemen. From these documents it will also be seen that the total outstanding securities which have been issued by the Canadian Northern and its allied companies amount to $311,276,822.32. Of this total the sum of $58,042,248 has been guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada and the sum of $76,850,203 has been guaranteed by various provincial governments. The balance which amounts to $176,383,371 represents securities which have been issued but which have not been guaranteed by governments.
The most profitable portion of the road now in operation consists of the lines extending from Port Arthur to Edmonton, and these lines, as hon. gentlemen are aware, are for the most part situated within the three prairie provinces. These lines however, are to-day less profitable than they otherwise would be until the system is extended, on the one hand to the Pacific coast, and on the other hand to Quebec and Montreal, so as to be in touch with the great traffic which has already developed, and which will develop in still greater measure, in the future, upon the Pacific ocean, and to bring the road into touch with the great railway systems of Ontario and Quebec, and particularly the system of government railways, and the Canadian Pacific railway system, so far as it is situated within Quebec and the Maritime provinces.
The Canadian Northern system, so-called, comprises the Canadian Northern Railway Company which owns the lines in the prairie provinces, and various subsidiary or allied companies -which are enumerated and set forth in the schedules to the resolution. The securities of many of these allied companies have been guaranteed by the Canadian Northern railway proper and thus the lines owned by the Canadian Northern railway proper in the prairie provinces, which undoubtedly are the profitable portion of the system from an operating standpoint, are vitally interested in the completion, extension and success of the whole system.
It became apparent some months ago that the enterprise could not be carried to a successful conclusion without further assistance. That assistance became necessary for various reasons, among which there was the financial stringency that for a year or eighteen months past has prevailed not only in Canada but-what is of more importance in this particular instance-in the great money markets of the world. The difficulty of making a successful flotation of issues already authorized and o£ further proposed

issues was so great that it could not be attempted without the risk of absolute failure. In the meantime, those who were carrying on the operation of the road so far as already constructed and who were endeavouring to bring the completion of the system to a successful issue, were confronted with this condition. The ordinary current indebtedness of the system, more especially in connection with operation, had increased from $3,000,000, its normal amount, to nearly $11,000,000. It was found that nearly $11,000,000 of contractors' accounts remained unpaid and could not be met. In addition to this, Mackenzie and Mann Limited had raised $10,500,000 to meet outstanding contractors' accounts. Under these circumstances, the company have presented to the Government the statement, which is found on page 10 of the printed documents and which indicates the amount necessary to be provided in order that the road may be completed. This balance of $41,905,117 must be provided for the completion of the road and for certain betterments which, as I understand, are absolutely required in the immediate future.
It may be asked why the $58,473,982, which is apparently available, cannot be used for the completion of the road. That seems to be a very natural question, and it. is one which I myself asked when the statement was first presented to me. The explanation is very simple, namely, that both subsidies and proceeds of securities are not available until expenditure has been made which justifies payment by the Minister of Finance or by the trustees for the bond-holders in the case of other trust securities. Subsidies as well as the proceeds of securities which are raised by means of guarantees are paid out only in the proportion which the expenditure bears to the total estimated cost of the road; and in respect of this railway and of all railways, the construction of which is provided for in part by subsidies and in part by the proceeds of bonds and securities, there is necessary as well what may be called a working construction capital; that is, money has to be provided for carrying on the work of the road, and capital is necessary for that purpose before either the proceeds of the securities which are lodged with a trustee or the amount of the subsidies earned can be made available.
The procedure, as I understand it, is as follows. In the first place, the Government engineers inspect the road from time to time and satisfy themselves as to the amount of expenditure which has been made upon it. They also make an estimate of the total cost of the road when completed. The subsidies are paid out only in the proportion which the expenditure incurred bears to the total estimated cost, and the same is true of the proceeds of guaranteed securities, that is securities guaranteed by the Government of Canada, the proceeds of which are always deposited with the Minister of Finance and the Receiver General. They are paid out in the same way, so that, when the last of the subsidies are paid, and when the last of the proceeds of guaranteed securities are paid, the road must have Teached [DOT]completion. I have made inquiry of various provincial governments as to the character of the legislation under which they afforded assistance to the road by way of guarantees. They have informed me that the procedure-is the same with them, namely that the proceeds of guaranteed securities are de-231
posited with the provincial treasurer and are paid only in the same proportion as that which I have already indicated with regard to federal subsidies and securities guaranteed by the federal government. Practically the same procedure is followed in respect of unguaranteed securities as well. The proceeds of those securities are deposited with the trustee for the bond-holders and are paid out by him only in the proportion which the amount actually expended, according to the report of the engineers, bears to the total estimated cost of the whole road. Therefore, while there were $58,473,982 of securities and subsidies apparently available, the difficulty with which the company found itself confronted was that, those subsidies not having been earned and the proceeds of those guaranteed securities not having been earned, it was impossible to apply those moneys to the construction of the road until further expenditures should have taken place thereon.
The extraordinary financial conditions above alluded to account in part, as I have said, for the need of further assistance, and the fact that the securities available cannot be sold at a reasonable price must also be taken into account. In addition to this there is undoubtedly an increased cost of the road due, as I am informed, and as I believe, after having made pretty careful inquiries into the matter, to two considerations: in the first place to a very decided advance in the price of labour and material during the past five or six years, and in the second place to the fact that a higher standard of construction has been adopted than that which was at first anticipated.
Now, the situation which was presented to the Government was not without its difficulties. The credit of the Dominion and of the several provinces had been pledged in very large amounts by the guarantee of securities. It had to be taken into account, and we did take it into account, that besides this the sum of nearly $180,000,000 was outstanding in unguaranteed securities, that that money had been invested in this enterprise by people who may have been influenced, and undoubtedly were influenced, by the fact that the road was recognized as a great transcontinental railway in Canada, and further, by the fact that the road had received very substantial assistance, not only from the federal Government, but from the provincial governments, both in subsidies and by the guarantee of securities. My attention was called recently to an article

in the Journal of Commerce of Montreal, under date of 6th May, which is not only entitled to respect by reason of the fact that a gentleman who has been very eminent in the public life of Canada for many years is supposed to preside over the editorial utterances of that journal- I refer to Hon. W. S. Fielding-but also is notable for the expression of opinion which it gives with regard to the duty of the Government in respect of the completion of this transcontinental railway. I will not read the whole article, but a portion of it might very well be quoted at this juncture:
No doubt many members on both sides of the House share the widespread feeling that both Dominion and provincial Legislatures have distributed aid in cash, land and guarantees to the railway companies with a rather lavish hand, and that there should be a slowing down, if, indeed, not a halt, in this generous policy. That members entertaining these views should be inclined to set their faces against further assistance to the Canadian Northern is quite natural. But there is another side to the question that must be considered by all who have a sense of responsibility.
Whether the railway aid policies of the past have been.too generous; whether governments, in their desire to provide for the railway needs of the opening west, have moved too rapidly; whether it was wise to become involved in the construction of a third transcontinental railway, while the second was still far from completion-these are questions upon which as one looks back at the events of the last few years, there may easily be room for wide difference of opinion. But such differences would not be sufficient ground for a refusal to face the conditions of the present time.
The affairs of a great railway company, which owes its existence to the encouragement given by Government and Parliament, become so interwoven with the general interests of the country, and particularly with the public credit in the money markets of the world, that it becomes impossible to regard them as matters of private concern. There was a time when the Canadian Pacific, with all the aid it had received, found itself in a critical position. The Government had to come to its aid, and although their action in so doing did not escape adverse criticism there will be few if any to say to-day that the help should not have been granted. The Grand Trunk Pacific has already more than once had to seek assistance. At this moment it is representing that, owing to the very large increase in the cost of labour, materials and supplies, the earlier estimates of the cost of the division which the company are building have been greatly exceeded, and that therefore the Government should make the public aid proportionately larger. The Canadian Northern, under one name or another, is operating in almost every province of Canada. Its financial stability is a matter of importance to a very large number of corporations and individuals with whom it has had dealings, and also to the public interests represented by Dominion and provincial Governments.
To allow the concern to fail in its finances and leave the various railway lines in an un-

finished state would be a national calamity that could not be seriously contemplated by any one possessed of a due sense of responsibility. The company, if it is in difficulty, as fs alleged, must be helped, and the only questions to be considered are the form and extent of the assistance and the proper means of protecting, as far as that may be possible, the Dominion in the way of security for the aid to be given.
Now, Mr. Speaker, many suggestions have naturally been made to the Government in connection with the action to be taken under the circumstances which have been brought to our attention. I start with a *premise with which I think every hon. gentleman in this House will agree, and that is that that system cannot he allowed to remain uncompleted. To leave a road upon which so much money has been expended, into which so much of the money of this Dominion and of the provinces has been poured, a road which has been endorsed by the financial guarantees, not only of the federal but of provincial governments-to leave that with two thousand or two thousand five hundred miles of road necessary to link up the whole system, in an unfinished condition, is a proposition to which no hon. gentleman on either side of the House would give his support and sanction. It was suggested to us, however, that the road should be allowed to go into liquidation, that its finances should be reorganized with a view to cutting down the amount of unguaranteed securities. I am free to admit that *that proposal never commended itself to .my judgment; and I say that, inasmuch as Canada is to-day in that condition of progress and development which makes it absolutely necessary that we should resort almost continuously to the money markets of the world, a saving of $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 or $50,000,000, if that were possible by that method, would in the end result in the loss of tenfold that sum to this country in view of its possible progress and development. It was apparent, as I have said, that the road could not remain uncompleted. It constitutes a part of a great projected transcontinental system and its traffic over the lines in operation has developed wonderfully during the last half dozen years and especially in the western provinces. To leave it uncompleted would retard the progress of this country for at least a generation; and as far as I can discern the situation, even if the road went into liquidation it could not he brought to completion within a reasonable delay unless this country should come to its assistance

by some such measure as this. Therefore, it seemed to us that under proper stipulations and under proper safeguards it was not only desirable but necessary for the country at this time to give such assistance as would insure the completion of that road at an early day.
Certain arguments against any assistance to the road were based also upon the connection of Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann with this enterprise. The undertaking, on which they embarked in 1896, and which had its inception in the construction of 100 miles of railway in the province of Manitoba, has gradually developed into the proposed construction of a great national transcontinental system. I am free to confess that I think it would have been better, when the idea of that enterprise became fixed in the minds of Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann, if they, by means of their large holdings of common stock and by their almost sole proprietorship of the enterprise, had seen fit in years gone by to associate themselves with large financial interests which, I think, could have been brought into the enterprise, so that the condition which confronts the country at this time might not have been before us to-day. I am saying no more here in Parliament than I have said, in terms even franker than those I have used here, to both Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann.
But there was more than that. It has been asserted in the press and in the corridors of this House, and noised abroad throughout the country that large sums of money which have been raised for the purposes of this undertaking, through federal or provincial government guarantees, and by means of unsecured bonds, have been appropriated not to the purpose for which they were raised but to the private enterprises of Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann. It is needless to say that if any such condition as that could, be found to prevail, it would demand immediate and drastic action by the Government and by Parliament. Further than that, it was alleged that Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann, as contractors for construction, had made very large profits out of the enterprise. Finally it was charged that the moneys raised, whether by Dominion guarantees, provincial guarantees, or without guarantees, had been improvidemtly expended or wasted. We thought it our duty, under the circumstances, to have the books 231i
and records of the system and, so far as it was necessary, other books and records investigated for the purpose of ascertaining whether or not there was any truth in the charge that moneys raised for the purpose of constructing this railway had been diverted to other enterprises. I am bound to say that the evidence which we have received, through the examination, inquiry and report of the expert auditors appointed by the Government, leads us to the conclusion that not one single dollar of the moneys raised has been diverted by Sir William Mackenzie or Sir Donald Mann to any other enterprise or appropriated to any other purpose than the construction of this road. We also felt it our duty to investigate, and we did investigate, the question as to whether or not profits had been rereceived by Mackenzie and Mann in respect of construction and whether or not the moneys expended had been prudently and providently used in the prosecution of the work. I think the extent of work which has been done and the amount which has been expended upon it, when contrasted with the results which have obtained in the case of other similar enterprises, whether in this country or in the United States, would reasonably lead one to the conclusion that the money has been prudently and providently and wisely expended. So far as profits are concerned, I have already placed upon the table of the House the report of the auditors, which indicate that no profits have been received by Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann out of the construction of the road; that they have been acting for some years past as construction agents for the Canadian Northern Railway system; that the only remuneration or compensation which they have received for their services up to the present time has been the allocation to them of common stock; but that they would, unless a safeguard had been provided by the resolution now proposed, have been legally entitled to a claim against the Canadian Northern Railway system of $15,000,000, $20,000,000 or perhaps $25,000,000 for the services which they have rendered, upon the ordinary basis of computation which I understand is applied to such cases. In saying that I desire hon. gentlemen in this House to realize that these two gentlemen have devoted 18 years of their lives almost entirely to the prosecution of this enterprise, which already has attained an important status in the transportation system of this country, and I

think it will be admitted that they have broughtto the prosecution of the work which they have undertaken an amount of ability and energy and skill which, perhaps, ha? not been exceeded in this country or in any other country in connection with the carrying on of such enterprises.
In addition to the report of the auditors, to which I have already alluded, we have a declaration from the comptroller of the company, Mr. Alfred James Mitchell, of the city of Toronto, who has had charge of the accounts and records of the Canadian Northern railway and of the Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited, and who has peculiar means of knowing of the matters in respect of which he deposes in this declaration. It is as follows:
In the matter of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. .
I, Alfred James Mitchell, of the city of Toronto, in the county of York, Esquire, do solemnly declare:	.
That I am the comptroller of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, and as such have a knowledge of the facts hereinafter stated.
MacKenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, have acted as contractors for the Canadian Northern Railway Company in the construction of certain of its lines and of certain allied lines, as per schedule 'A' attached hereto.
It will not be necessary for me to read the schedule. (Reading):
In connection with the construction to date of such lines, I say that to the best of my knowledge and belief and according to the books kept by me as such comptroller, no contractors' profits or percentage had been received directly or indirectly by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, or by any other person on their behalf or for their profit, save and except certain fully paid common stock ot the said Canadian Northern Railway Company and of its allied lines issued to them from time to time, the question as to payment for services or profits being left open for future adjustment.
The moneys received to December 31, 1913, by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, for railway construction as aforesaid amount in all to the sum of two hundred and twenty three million, four hundred and seven thousand, six hundred and forty one dollars and ninety eight cents ($223,407,641.98) and the whole of the moneys so received have been paid out by the Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, for construction of the said railway lines leaving no profit to them other than the said common stock.
And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing it to be true and knowing that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath and by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act.
