I am not concerned here to speak in any sense on behalf of Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, or Sir William Mackenzie, or Sir Donald Mann. The question that we have to -discuss and consider in Parliament at this juncture is one which transcends the interest of any individual in the country. It is a national question and one which must be looked at from a national standpoint only. It is, however, proper to say that it has been represented to us that

Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann have put into this enterprise very large assets which they might, under the law of the land, have retained for their own benefit in the earlv stages of the development of this system. The Lake Manitoba Railway and Canal Company was, I think, the name of the company whose charter they first acquired. Then came the Winnipeg and Hudson Bay railway and the Manitoba and Southeastern Railway Company, and perhaps some other companies in Manitoba, It is fair to say that the charters of these companies had gone begging for half a dozen years before Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann took hold of them, and during all those years no man had ever come forward to carry out the particular enterprises in connection with these companies which Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann did carry out. It is perfectly well understood by hon. gentlemen in this House [DOT] familiar with such matters that these charters carried with them large land grants, and that it would have been possible for any man in Canada to have acquired those charters and, by the construction of those roads, to have acquired the lands which were granted as a subsidy in aid of that construction if he had seen fit to do so. Mr. Mackenzie and Mr. Mann came forward and acquired those charters and, by the construction of the roads, acquired also lands of very great extent, amounting, I think, to over four million acres in all, which at the time when they were acquired were probably of very little value and possibly could not have been sold at all, but which eventually, through the development and progress of the country, have acquired a very substantial and indeed a very large value.
I think it ought to be said in justice to these men that all those lands, which under the law of the land they might have retained if they had desired to do so as their cwn property absolutely, were not retained by them, with the exception, I believe, of one hundred thousand acres, but were placed into this enterprise. The amount already realized from these lands is $17,000,000 and upwards, which has been added to the assets of the Canadian Northern Railway system. There is enough of these lands left to provide, at current prices, something like $12,000,000 more. So it ought to be said, in fairness to these men, that, hav ing the right to retain these lands and to retire from railway construction as men with very large fortunes, they had the ambition to construct a great national transcontinental railway system and into that system they placed the $29,000,000 of assets to which I have just alluded, being the proceeds of the lands which they acquired from the construction of those three lines of railway. I have no doubt that the original idea and ambition of these gentlemen was to make large fortunes out of the construction of railways, and that they did not have in their minds any idea of constructing the great transcontinental system which is almost complete to-day. But it would seem to me that the course taken by them indicates that many years ago the mere idea of making a large fortune out of this, enterprise ceased to be their sole purpose; that they did desire as well to build a transcontinental railway line which would be an important factor in the railway development of this country.
In connection with their idea of building a national transcontinental railway system this also may fairly be said. I have heard it charged against them that if they had been contented simply to develop their lines in the three Prairie provinces and not to reach out to the West, they would have had a very profitable railway system in western Canada and one which would have been of very great service to the country. I think it is only fair that I should give it to the House that their idea in making their eastern extension was that, previously to the projection of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, they had in eastern Canada a road, the Grand Trunk railroad, with no western connections, with which they could make a working arrangement and provide for an interchange of traffic upon reasonable terms. But when the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway project was brought about they found themselves confronted with this situation: They had to meet the competition of two great railway systems reaching into the east as well as into the west of Canada, and so they would have been isolated in their operations, they would have been handicapped and might have been oppressed. For the reason that the second transcontinental railway was launched in that way they had the belief, whether it was right or wrong, that, in the very nature of things, it was essential for them to press on into eastern Canada.
It was necessary also for us to go into the question of. future earnings and future expenditures, for betterments or otherwise, because these betterments would undoubtedly be necessary even if the road should

be completed. The anticipation of the company as to earnings after the completion of the system is to be found on page 14 of the printed documents, and upon the same page is to be found a statement of the earnings of the company during the last fiscal year. In considering the possibility of the system acquiring earning power sufficient to meet its total fixed charges, we sought the advice of engineering and traffic experts of the'Intercolonial railway. It is obvious that the future earning power of the system will depend on the progress and development of the country and the future expenditures for bettermems on traffic necessities. While it is possible that the expectations of the company, which are very sanguine, may not be realized, it must, nevertheless, be remembered that the system at present has an earning power equal to that of the Canadian Pacific railway in 1901, and if the country develops in the future as in the past, of which we can have no reasonable doubt, the earning power of the system may be expected to increase accordingly. More than that, we are informed that the line from Montreal to Port Arthur and from Edmonton to the Pacific coast is of a high character, and will lend itself to low operating charges.
The main consideration which influenced us in placing these proposals before the House was the necessity for the completion of the road. We were impressed by the fact that liquidation must invollve long and serious delay in the completion of the enterprise, and must materially retard the development of the country. We were impressed by the fact that such liquidation would impose serious charges and burdens not only upon the federal exchequer, but upon the provincial treasuries. We were impressed by the fact that very large sums, amounting to many millions, were owing to contractors, subcontractors, merchants, material men, and labourers throughout Canada. And we were impressed also by this fact: that a reasonable confidence in the future development of the country should lead to the belief that the enterprise could be carried to a successful conclusion. It has been suggested that adequate provision has not been made in the resolutions which we propose for the payment of contractors and labourers. So far as labour is concerned, there is already in chapter 98 of the Revised Statutes of Canada most ample provision. So far as the resolutions are concerned, although I do not intend to go into any argument upon that point at the moment, I may call the attention of hon. 
gentlemen to the fact that under clause 6 of the resolutions it is provided that the dispositions of the moneys to he raised by means of the guaranteed securities shall be such as the Governor in Council approves; and we shall take care that all contractors, material men and others who have made advances or to whom debts are owing shall be fully protected in connection with the completion of this road.
The road when completed will have an indebtedness of about $40,000 a mile, and fixed charges of $1,600 per mile, which I think will compare very favourably with other systems in this country 4 p.m. and the United States. Undoubtedly, if conditions had permitted it, it would have been desirable to organize a new corporation which would take over the assets and undertakings of all the various companies which form part of the system. We are convinced, however, that by reason of the methods of financing adopted in the past, the great variety of securities issued, and for similar reasons which seemed cogent to us, it is impossible to accomplish this at the present moment. Nevertheless, we required, so far as it was practicable, that all the lines constituting the system should be brought under one management, and in effect amalgamated. The method which has been adopted accomplishes this result in effect while at the same time it does not affect the priority of charges or liens which have been created in the past, and which eventually may, under some refunding arrangement, be arranged so as to permit the entire ownership of the lines to be vested in one corporation. In that regard I would like to say that the Government have 'been careful to see that every security which could have been made available through amalgamation, has been acquired.
The total capitalization of the various companies amounts to $138,500,000, and further proposed capitalization of the Montreal Terminals and of the Canadian Northern Manitoba railway would bring that amount up to about $145,000,000. The total capitalization of the system has been reduced to $100,000,000 by the following method: The stock of all the subsidiary and constituent companies-to which I shall allude as the allied companies-has been transferred to the Canadian Northern railway, and the capitalization of that company has been fixed at $100,000,000. The several companies are prohibited from any further issue of stock.

The proposed issue of $45,000,000 is to be made by the Canadian Northern railway- the parent company to which all the stock of the allied companies is to be transferred-and the Government is to be safeguarded against any liability upon this guarantee by the following securities:
1.	A mortgage upon the undertaking, property, assets and revenues of the Canadian Northern railway, which comprises some 5,3o0 miles, extending between Port Arthur and Edmonton, and includes numerous branches in the three prairie provinces.
2.	A mortgage or charge upon the properties and assets of the allied companies to the extent to which any of the moneys raked by the guaranteed securities may be appropriated and paid for construction or betterment of their respective undertakings.
3.	A mortgage or charge upon the shares of the allied companies now transferred to the Canadian Northern.
4.	A charge upon all the securities and stocks enumerated in the second schedule, and a first charge upon the Brockville and Westport railway-a small railway of about 45 miles.
5.	A charge upon the equity of redemption of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, in $10,000,000 of capital stock, and $10,000,000 of first debenture stock in the Canadian Northern Town Properties, Limited.
Some further explanation may be given at a later date with regard to the value of that security. We regard it as very valuable security indeed.
In addition to twenty-one million dollars now owing in respect of construction, the Canadian Northern and its allied companies have incurred liabilities to the extent of $20,703,865 -as shown on page 112 of the documents brought down-upon temporary loans secured by the deposit or pledge of securities which under present conditions are not saleable at a reasonable price.
The fourth section of the resolution provides that covenants or undertakings to the satisfaction of the Government shall be given by Mackenzie and Mann, Limited; that these loans shall be paid, and that no proceedings against the Canadian Northern ox any of the allied companies shall be taken in respect thereof. Our idea in that regard is this: we are guaranteeing $45,000,000 worth of securities, as asked for by the memorandum which I read to the House in the early portion of my remarks, to ensure the completion of
this road. When we found that these temporary loans were outstanding to the extent mentioned, that they were secured merely by the pledge of certain bonds and debentures, we made it a stipulation that these temporary loans should be taken care of by Mackenzie and Mann-not by the country- and that the proceeds of the $45,000,000 of guaranteed securities should be available for the completion of the road, and not used to pay off these temporary loans.
In addition to this indebtedness it has been found that the current indebtedness of the Canadian Northern and allied companies, the normal amount of which would be in the vicinity of three million dollars, has risen to the sum of $10,408,128.30. The Government have exacted a stipulation- which is to be found in the fifth clause of the resolution-that security to the satisfaction of the Government shall be given by Mackenzie and Mann and by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited-not only their own covenant, but such further security as the Government may demand- that this indebtedness will, within one year, be reduced to the normal or usual current amount, which is to be determined by the minister, and that in the meantime no proceedings shall be taken against the company for payment of the same. The giving of such guarantees or securities in respect of the temporary loans and of the current indebtedness are made conditions precedent to any guarantee by the Government.
We have also provided by clause 9 of the resolution that the books, returns, reports and other records of the Canadian Northern and allied companies shall at all times be accessible and open to inspection by competent experts appointed by the Government.
In that connection and for a similar reason, we have provided that the Government shall have authority to appoint a director of the Canadian Northern and a director of each of the allied companies, and that the Government shall have power to remove any such director and to appoint another director in his stead. Such director shall have the power to cause meetings of directors or shareholders to be held at any time, and in that way we believe that the Government will be kept fully in touch with and fully acquainted with the proposals of the management and the condition of the undertaking from time to time.
For further safeguard we have also pro-

vided that the company shall, within five months after the close of each fiscal year, furnish to the Government a balance sheet showing the financial condition of the Canadian Northern Railway System for the year then completed.
As the system has long since assumed the status of a transcontinental railway, we considered it important that all companies whose lines are included in the system .should he brought within the legislative jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada and made subject to the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. This has been accomplished by section 15 of the Bill, which will follow the resolution. My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) urged that point upon us, when certain proposals affecting this company were under consideration by Parliament last year. We have thought it desirable that this provision should be inserted, not only with regard to the company to which he called attention then, and which indeed was the only company under consideration at the time, but that it should also be applied to all those companies which are not at present subject to the legislative jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada and which form part of the Canadian Northern system.
The Government have thought it desirable in the public interest and for the reasons already stated, that the road should not be permitted to go into liquidation. Nevertheless, as the contingent liability which is imposed upon the people of the country by the proposals which are now before the House is a substantial one, we have held it to be reasonable that the people of this country, lending their credit for the completion of this enterprise, should also directly participate in any profits and advantages of the enterprise if it is carried to a successful completion. Therefore, in fixing the total capitalization of the Canadian Northern Railway system at $100,000,000 we have required that $40,000,000 thereof shall be absolutely vested in the Government as trustees for the people of Canada who will thus participate in any value which may eventually accrue through the progress and development of the country.
I venture to say that there is no man in this House or in this country who will deny that the people of Canada, in coming to the assistance of this enterprise at this juncture, are reasonably entitled to file compensation which we have asked for in these proposals and upon which we intend to insist. The capitalization of the whole sys-

tem, when these negotiations commenced, stood approximately at $145,000,000 of which $138,000,000 were held by Mackenzie and Mann and $7,000,000 were held by the Government. In consideration of the assistance now afforded to the enterprise, this capitalization has been reduced to $100,000,000 of which $60,000,000 are held by the former proprietors and $40,000,000 are held by the Government. The stock of Mackenzie and Mann has thus been reduced by $68,000,000 and the stock of the Government has been increased by $33,000,000. To permit the road to go into liquidation would not only injure seriously the credit of all Canadian enterprises and of Canada itself for many years, but would involve long delay in the completion of the enterprise.

Before the right hon. gentleman leaves that question of stock, I would like to understand what the effect of subsection I of section 12 of the agreement has, in providing for the issue of $25,000,000 additional stock for the purpose of retiring income.

The next letter is from the Hon. J. A. Calder, acting premier of the province of Quebec, under date of Ottawa, April 17, 1914:
Dear Mr. Borden:
As I have been advised that you are not expected to return to Ottawa until next Monday or Tuesday, and as I must leave for the West on Friday, I regret that I shall not have another opportunity of discussing with you the question of further federal aid to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Since our last conference I have given the matter a good deal of consideration and now wish to communicate to you briefly the general conclusions I have reached.
As I understand the situation, the company in question has made application to your Government for further Dominion aid, chiefly, if not solely, on the ground that such aid is required to enable it to complete and put into operation its main line through British Columbia and east of Port Arthur, thereby providing the necessary outlets for the network of branch lines which the company has constructed throughout the prairie regions.
Regarding the necessity which may exist for the assistance applied for I have no opinion to offer as I have no knowledge of the facts. On the other hand, however, it appears to me that there can be no room for a difference of opinion as to the desirability of having the company carry to completion its through lines at the earliest possible date, more especially as these eastern and western outlets for the products of the prairies have already been largely provided for and are approaching completion.
I have already given you my views with respect to the absolute necessity which exists for the immediate construction of additional branch railways in Saskatchewan. If you desire confirmation of the same I would refer you to the recent decision of the Board of Railway Commissioners in the western freight rates case. The whole question was investigated thoroughly by the board and their conclusions, as well as their reasons therefore will be found embodied in their report.
Viewing the matter, therefore, from this standpoint, it seems to me that if there is any likelihood that the Canadian Northern railway, on account of the magnitude of its through line undertakings may without additional federal assistance, be left in such a position as to compel it to curtail or hold back its branch line development, the loss to western Canada would be very great indeed.

be more effectively safeguarded we shall be glad to consider suggestions to that end. The commitments of Canada in aiding transcontinental railways are very great. I will not pause to consider their wisdom, as the hour for that has passed. The collapse of this enterprise would undoubtedly be a national calamity. It may well be added that lack of courage in dealing with it would be a national disgrace. The enterprise must proceed, but the interest of the country coming to its assistance must be considered and it has been considered. Every dollar of the money to be raised by means of the securities which we propose to guarantee will be used for the payment of existing liabilities of the Canadian Northern system and for the completion of the road. If the expectations of those who believe the enterprise can be carried to a successful conclusion are disappointed, then a summary method has been provided by which the road can be taken over, the system reorganized and either be transferred to another corporation constituted for the purpose, or pass intc the ownership of the people. If, on the other hand, the enterprise meets with the anticipated success, the country will have acquired a two-fifths interest therein as compensation for the guarantee of forty-five millions of dollars. The Canadian Northern system to-day has earnings equivalent tc those of the Canadian Pacific railway! in 1901. We all confidently hope, and, more than that, believe that the progress and development of Canada during the next twelve years will not be less than that with which this Dominion .has been favoured since 1901. In that case it may reasonably be anticipated that the compensation now received from the company for the aid proposed by these resolutions will amply recoup and compensate Canada for every subsidy and guarantee that it has brought to the assistance of this railway. It may not be amiss to bear in mind that a like policy applied thirty years ago in affording assistance to the Canadian Pacific railway would have most amply recouped the country for all its aid to that great undertaking. And so to-day our faith in the future progress and development of this Dominion impels us to believe that for the assistance now proposed the country is receiving a consideration which in the years to come will more than amply compensate not only for the pledge of the country's credit which we now propose, but for all other aid which 
ha^ been granted to this enterprise-and in both cases the country has secured also the construction of a great transcontinental railway.

Mr. Speaker,
in rising to present the views which I and those with whom I am associated on this side of-the House entertain with regard to the resolution which has' been presented to the House, I hope that I shall not be considered as making a vain boast if I say that it is our firm purpose to approach this question with minds as free as they can be from consideration of party interest considerations which are never absolutely devoid of passion, and to give to this very important question the attention to which it is entitled, and upon its merits alone.
I may confess at once that I have long believed that this country requires thTee transcontinental railways and although this theory has been sometimes controverted, in this House and out of it, I have never seen any reason to change my opinion. The Americans have three transcontinental railways, the Union Pacific, which is the oldest, the Great Northern and the Southern Pacific, and these three are scarcely adequate to meet the needs of the enormous trade which they have to carry. It is no vain boast to say that in prospects our western country is certainly equal, if not superior, to the western part of the American Republic. Not the whole but the greater part of the American territory west of the Mississippi river is a barren desert which is and must for all time remain unproductive, whereas our own country west of lake Superior is, every inch of it, not only arable but fertile, and not only fertile, but fertile as few other countries are. For my part I can say that I have always favoured the efforts of our two fellow citizens whose names have been mentioned several times by my right hon. friend, and who have applied themselves for many years to the task of binding the continent with another band of steel. The late Government were not slow to interest themselves in the enterprise and to favour it as much as they could. The beginnings of the railway system which we are now considering were certainly very modest, and I doubt if even its projectors, Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann, thought at that time that their system would attain the proportions which it has since atained. It was, as has been stated by my right hon. friend, in the year 1696 that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann went into railway construction. It is to their very great credit that the first venture which
MAY i3, 1914
they took up was an enterprise which, had gone a-begging and which nobody dared to tackle at that time. With the assistance of the provincial Government of Manitoba., they started the construction of a small line of railway branching out. north and west from the existing system. In 1899, or thereabouts, after we came into office, we asked Parliament to give them assistance to extend the railway system then in existence in Manitoba eastward to the end of lake Superior. If I remember rightly, we gave them a cash subsidy of $6,400 a mile for that length of railway. Later, in 1903, we induced Parliament to give them a guarantee of $13,000 a mile for a line of railway running through Manitoba to the city of Edmonton. Afterwards, in 1908, we asked Parliament to give them another guarantee of bonds to provide for several branch lines which wTould be feeders of the line in the prairie provinces. In 1911, as has been explained by my right hon. friend, it was considered that the system would not be complete unless it were extended eastward to the St. Lawrence and eventually to the Maritime provinces, that is to say, unless it were made a transcontinental railway, and in that year we asked Parliament to give to the enterprise from Port Arthur to Montreal a guarantee of bonds to the extent of $25,000 a mile. After the new Government came into office they took up the policy which we inaugurated. In 1912 Parliament was asked to assist a line from St. Albert to the limits of the province of British Columbia, a distance of 115 miles, with a subsidy of $35,000 a mile. They also asked and got from this Parliament a cash subsidy of $12,000 per mile in British Columbia, for a distance of 525 miles. I for my part, and those around me, -did not assist in that last vote, for reasons which I shall explain later on. Last year the Government again extended its bounty to the enterprise and Parliament granted it a cash subsidy from Ottawa to Port Arthur, a distance of 910 miles, of $12,000 per mile, or $10,920,000; and from Edmonton to the boundary of British Columbia, a distance of 260 miles, a cash subsidy of $12,000 per mile, amounting to $3,120,000; in all, $14,040,000. Thus, since the present Government came into office, this enterprise has been assisted to the extent of $24,365,000, of which $4,000,000 was only a guarantee, while $20,040,000 was actual cash. Last year, when my right hon. friend asked the bounty of Parliament for the enterprise, he expressed his opinion-I shall not say conviction, but his strong opinion, or rather the opinion of the promoters of the enterprise, Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann-that with the assistance which we were then giving them, they would he in a position to complete the enterprise by the borrowings which they could make elsewhere. Unfortunately, as we know, these sanguine expectations have not been realized, and they are again before us for a further bounty from Parliament, which, as they again assert, will enable them to complete their system.
It has been current in the corridors of this House, in clubs, in the streets, and in the press all over the country, that the Canadian Northern Company was stranded financially, that the owners of it could not advance any more-nay, that there were against them millions upon millions of liabilities due to their contractors, to their furnishers, to the banks, which they were unable to meet. It was stated also that, unless the country came to their assistance, we were threatened with a financial crisis. It was represented to us that the situation was pretty much the same as the situation in 1884 when the promoters of the Canadian Pacific railway came before Parliament and asked for a loan of $30,000,000 in order to face liabilities which they were unable to meet, and thus avoid a financial crisis. If, Sir, these rumours, which we have heard every day almost since the opening of the session four months ago, had been realized, if it was true that the finances of the company were in such a condition that they could not meet their liabilities, that their credit was exhausted, and that possibly, unless assistance were afforded to them, some financial institution might be in serious peril, involving the fall of some other institutions not so strong, the condition- of things would be far different from the condition of things stated by my right hon. friend. If the situation to-day were the same as it was in 1884, as we had expected, if the promoters of-the enterprise had represented to us that they were for the moment financially embarrassed, that in view of the conditions of the financial market they could not realize any more upon the securities which they had in hand, and that unless we came to their rescue we might have to face a financial crisis, I for my part, would have been inclined to favour doing exactly what was done by Parliament in 1884-lend them the money in order to avoid that financial crisis. But, Sir, this is not the condition which is pre-

sented to us to-day. This is not the statement which is made by the promoters of the enterprise, Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann. They do not represent at all that they are unable to meet their liabilities. They say, on the contrary, and it is stipulated in the resolutions-and my right hon. friend has just insisted upon this point- that the money which is to be raised on the guarantee which they ask of us is not to go to the payment of their liabilities, but is for another object. Indeed, when the resolution was laid before the House some days ago, a communication coming from the Government was given to the ministerial press in which you could read this:
As the company, outside of the amounts owed to contractors, which are very large at the present time, owes also about $14,000,000 of temporary loans raised by the pledging of securities which have not been sold and which hitherto have not been saleable at a reasonable figure, and as the company has also floating indebtedness of between $10,000,000 and $11000,000, the Government have stipulated that Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, shall give absolutely satisfactory security that both the temporary loan and the floating indebtedness shall be paid off by them without recourse in any way to the moneys which are to be raised by the guaranteed securities for the completion of the road.
Therefore it is very plain that not a dollar of the money which is to be raised upon our credit is to go to discharge the liabilities of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann or of the Canadian Northern railway at the present moment. Indeed, the resolution which we have before us is to this effect in so many words. Let me read again the paragraphs which were read by my right hon. friend, and which go to show that the money which is to be raised upon our credit is not at all for the discharge of past liabilities. Sections 4 and 5 read:
4.	That covenants or undertakings to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council shall be given that all outstanding temporary loans to the Canadian Northern or any of its constituent or subsidiary companies secured by the deposit or pledge of securities, will be paid out of the proceeds of such deposited or pledged securities when the same shall be sold or disposed of, and that no proceedings against the Canadian Northern or any of said other companies will meanwhile be taken for the collection of such temporary loans.
5.	That covenants or undertakings of the contractors and such other covenants or undertakings as may be required by the Governor in Council shall be given that the current indebtedness of the Canadian Northern and of the said constituent and subsidiary companies will within one year from the passing of the Act to be based upon these resolutions be reduced to the normal or usual current amount to be determined by the minister and that

meanwhile all such current indebtedness other than such as may be the subject of bona fide dispute, will be either paid or arranged in such a manner that no proceedings for the enforcement of payment thereof will be taken or pressed.
Mark the difference between the language which I have just quoted and that of the statement which was given to the press. According to the press statement, security was to be given to the Government. Now, it is not security, but is simply a covenant which is given to the Government, that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, the Canadian Northern railway, the debtors whoever they be, shall r ot be pressed by their creditors. That is to say, they undertake to pay their creditors, or to have from them satisfactory arrangements that they will not be pressed; in other words, they will have an extension of time. I fail to understand the meaning of this resolution. If the debtors, those who owe this money, whoever they may be, whether the firm of Mackenzie and Mann or the Canadian Northern or any of the subsidiary companies, can make a covenant with the Government that their creditors shall not press them, they can make that agreement just as well with their creditors as with the Government. I do not understand how they can make it with the Government unless they make it also with their creditors; and, if they make it with their creditors, I do not see that there is any necessity of their making such an agreement with the Government. But be this as it may, this clearly is shown that the money to be raised by the sale of the securities is not to be used in paying off past liabilities.
This brings us, to the consideration of the reason why Parliament is asked to appropriate this sum of $45,000,000. At this juncture, I do not propose to go very deeply into the subject, but I intend to lay before Parliament in plain language the reasons why we on this side of the House think that these resolutions are absolutely unacceptable. If the object of the Government in asking for this credit of $45,000,000 is not that the company may discharge its present liabilities, if it is to continue to carry the load it has at the present time, and which it is unable to discharge, what is the reason why we are asked for this guarantee? The object is recited in the preamble to the resolution which is before the House:
Whereas the Canadian Northern Railway Company hereinafter called the ' Canadian Northern ' has represented that the several companies set forth in the first schedule to these resolutions, and their railways and un-

dertakings, rolling stock, equipment, assets and properties are intended to constitute a transcontinental railway system to be denominated the ' Canadian Northern system ' and that the Canadian Northern desires to control said system by the ownership or control of the shares of majorities thereof in the capital stock of the said companies, and that it now owns or controls the shares or majorities thereof in the capital stock of certain of the said companies, and that the several companies are desirous that aid should be granted for the purpose of completing the construction and equipment of the works and undertakings of the Canadian Northern system and for the betterment thereof.
So that, according to the language which I have just quoted, the main object of the Government in asking for this credit is to unite the different companies which at present are already under the ownership of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann. If that be the object, it is not sufficient
5 p.m. for asking us to appropriate $45,000,000; and, if that be not the object, then we must know that reason, I say that we should know the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Moreover, that is not all. We are told that these companies are to be united in a transcontinental system, and with that object I agree; but I say that object is not carried out in these resolutions. In the system as it exists at the present time there are twenty-eight different companies. When this resolution has passed, and when the Act founded on it has received the sanction of the Governor General'-if it receive it

there will still be twenty-eight different companies as there are at present. Why is this? My hon. friend told us a moment ago that the capital stock of twenty-seven of these companies is to go into company under Mackenzie and Mann. That may be the intention. I heard from my right hon. friend a moment ago that the capital stock was to be reduced to $100,000,000. I say that if that be the intention, it is not at all expressed in the resolution before the House. On the contrary, 'by the resolutions now before us the twenty-eight companies preserve their identity. The stock of twenty-seven companies goes into the hands of one company, it may be; but the twenty-eight different companies remain fully alive. Why is this? If you are going to give the stock of twenty-seven of the companies into the hands of one company, why not wipe them out altogether? I repeat that, if it is the intention to reduce the stock of these 28 different companies to $100,000,000, that intention is not expressed in this resolution, and the resolution will have to be
amended accordingly. Let me call the attention of my right hon. friend to that point. I do not know who prepared the resolutions, but whoever did it did not carry out the intention of the Government as it has been announced to us by my right hon. friend this afternoon. Take the language of the resolution, which seems to have been prepared with care. It reads:
In the following resolutions, unless the context otherwise requires:
'Canadian Northern' means the Canadian Northern Railway Company.
* Constituent companies ' means such of those companies mentioned in the first schedule to the following resolutions, and such other companies, hereafter declared by the Governor in Council to he comprised in the Canadian Northern system, as own or operate railways, terminals, bridges or other railway facilities.

The distinction between constituent companies and subsidiary companies is very minute, and a definition perhaps, was not necessary to an understanding of what was meant. I call these companies subsidiary companies, whether constituent or subsidiary; they are practically the same. I would call the attention of my right hon. friend to section 12, which says:
That the capital stock of the Canadian Northern be fixed at the sum of one hundred million dollars subject to increase only by the - Parliament of Canada.
What is the Canadian Northern? The Canadian Northern is not the Canadian Northern system; the, Canadian Northern is one company to which the other companies are accessories, and its capital stock is fixed at $100,000,000. I say this $100,000,000 cannot include the capital stock of the subsidiary companies, because the terms are against it.
But that is not all. I take the contract, of which clause 12 says:
That the contractors Mackenzie and Mann will forthwith, upon the execution hereof, transfer or cause to be transferred to the trustee all the shares of capital stock of constituent and subsidiary companies mentioned in the first and second parts of the schedule hereto, and the said shares shall form part of the mortgaged premises comprised in the new trust deed. .	.
The absolute ownership of all the shares mentioned in the first part of the said schedule shall be vested in the Canadian Northern, subject only to the charge thereon created by and to the terms of the new trust deed ;
And, therefore, if the capital stock of the subsidiary companies is to be transferred to

the Canadian Northern, they transfer something more than $100,000,000.
There is something else. By section 2, paragraph b, as security for the $45,000,000 we are advancing to Mackenzie and Mann, we receive a specific mortgage or charge upon the shares mentioned in the first part of the second schedule, that is to say, upon the stock of the subsidiary companies. If, therefore, we receive a mortgage upon the stock of the subsidiary companies, surely it cannot be contended that the stock of these subsidiary companies is wiped out. That is as plain as plain can be.
But there is something else. We receive also a mortgage upon this stock, but part of the stock of ten of these subsidiary companies is mortgaged to different creditors to the extent of $18,000,000. Are we to understand that you are wiping out the shares of these companies which are already secured for the protection of creditors who - advanced money upon them? That is the situation in which we are; and therefore it is very important to know exactly where we are at.
If it was the intention of the Government to have a transcontinental system, why have they preserved the identity of these companies? Why not wipe out their stock altogether? And if you do, there is nothing left of them except the board of management. Therefore, I say to my right hon. friend that if that be the idea he had really in mind, this resolution will have to be amended very carefully. But that is a point for consideration later on.
There is another point, and it is that if it was the intention of the Government to wipe out the stock of all these companies and to assimilate them and make them one, I shall insist that that intention shall be carried out in deed, and that we shall have one company and not twenty-eight companies. And since it is stated that the stock is of these twenty-eight companies is wiped out. I will ask whoever follows me to explain why we keep the identity of these twenty-eight companies which are not to disappear, the mortgage powers of which still remain and which are still empowered to exercise all their powers, and this will lead to very ludicrous consequences'. It is stipulated in section 18:
That without limiting any power now possessed, it be enacted that any constituent company which is now or may hereafter be subjc t to the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, may, under the provision of the Railway Act, amalgamate with any other it others of the constituent companies which is

Let us analyse what this means. It is stipulated that the stock, say, of the Canadian Northern Pacific Railway Company, is to be owned by the Canadian Northern Railway Company, which is practically Mackenzie and Mann. It is stipulated also that the stock of the Canadian Alberta Company is to be owned by the same parties, and therefore you provide that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, representing the Canadian Northern Pacific Company, can negotiate for amalgamation with Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, representing the Canadian Northern Alberta Company. If you have the power to amalgamate, why not amalgamate now, and make it clear once and for all? I confess I do not understand what is meant by so much confusion thrown into this agreement. If you want to have a transcontinental railway, as you say, why not enact so when you have the power?
But there is something more serious. For this charge of $45,000,000 which we are asked to vote to the Canadian Northern Railway Company, what security do we get? I submit with all confidence that the mortgage which we get as security is altogether illusory. Is my language too strong? Let me analyse what it means. Here is what we get as security for the $45,000,000 which we are asked to vote to that company:	First, as the resolution
reads, a grant of the first fixed specific mortgage or charge upon the shares, mentioned in the first part, of the subsidiary companies. We are now told that we are going to get a grant of a mortgage upon the stock and shares of the subsidiary companies; and yet we were told a moment ago that all the stock is wiped out. There is $81,000,000 of stock in these companies, and we are told it is altogether wiped out; therefore what becomes of our mortgage upon that stock? I shall be glad to be told what this means; but for my part I say it is absolutely illusory. Even if there were something left, even if the stock were not wiped out, what value would it have in the market to-day? It is of course impossible to speculate as to that. But I do know that while the stock pledged in this part of the agreement is to-day nominally worth $81,000,000, there is, what is not nominal, an indebtedness of $18,000,000 upon it. That is the true situation.
What do we get next? We get a specific

and floating mortgage or charge on the undertaking of the Canadian Northern and its properties, assets, rents and revenues, and its rights, powers, and franchises, present antd future. That would seem to be a mortgage upon the undertaking, upon the roadbed and upon the revenue, and that is worth a good deal, I admit. But we must not forget that against that same property there is a mortgage to-day of 3312,000,000. Does any one on the other side of the House believe that a mortgage upon the top of that mortgage for $312,000,000 is worth a great deal to Canada? Why, if we undertook to execute our rights under that mortgage we ourselves would simply have to provide for the payment of this $312,000,000. That is the consequence of the mortgage we are taking now, and it is the clearest part of it.
I have been tolfd: Oh, but you yourselves advanced money to this enterprise. So we did, but in every case we took a first mortgage. When we advanced in 1903 a certain amount per mile for the railway from Manitoba to Edmonton, we took a first mortgage upon that part of the road, and that mortgage is secure; it is as good as gold. When in 1908 we gave a further advance for another part of the road, we took also a first mortgage upon that part of the road which was to be created by our bounty, and we took a second mortgage upon this enterprise also. When in 1911 we gave a guarantee of bonds to the extent of $35,000 a mile to the enterprise from Port Arthur to Montreal, we took a first mortgage on that part of the road, and we also took a second mortgage on the whole of the enterprise. I venture to assert that even that second mortgage is perfectly satisfactory, though not so sure as the other one. According to this resolution, we have a general mortgage upon this enterprise, but we have not a similar mortgage upon the properties of the subsidiary companies. Somebody perhaps may say that I am wrong in this-that we have a mortgage for this $45,000,000 upon the properties of the subsidiary companies. I say no. We have a mortgage on the properties of the Canadian Northern Railway Company; we have not a mortgage upon the properties of the twenty-eight subsidiary companies. I assert this without any hesitation.
There is also in clause 11 a very extraordinary provision, namely, that, of this $45,000,000 which we are to raise upon our credit, that portion which goes into any one of these subsidiary enterprises for instance, 232
the Canadian Northern Alberta Railway Company, the Canadian Northern Manitoba Railway Company, the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan Railway Company, or the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company-is to be secured, not upon the whole of the enterprise, but upon that particular part of the enterprise. I do not understand the reason of this provision, but it is in the resolution.
We have been told in the preamble to this resolution that the object is to create a transcontinental railway, and that we are making an advance of $45,000,000 for this enterprise. If we are to do so, it seems to me to stand to reason that we should obtain a mortgage on the whole of the enterprise, and not simply on a part of it. We should obtain a guarantee upon the properties, not only of the Canadian Northern, but of the Canadian Northern Pacific, the Canadian Northern Alberta, the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan-of all the twenty-eight subsidiary companies that we are to amalgamate. Instead of having this guarantee upon the properties of these twenty-eight companies, we have a mortgage upon the properties of one of them, and the other twenty-seven will give separate mortgages for the part of the $45,000,000 which goes into their own territory. If this is an amalgamation, if this is the way in which you can have a transcontinental railway, I think it is a novel method. It is a method which is not conducive to the object you have in view. Therefore one of the reasons why I object to this resolution is that although it purports to constitute a transcontinental railway, it does nothing of the kind.
My right hon. friend said, and I altogether agree with him, that we cannot allow this enterprise to fail. We have too much money in it-not only the money of the country, but of the provinces and of the bond-holders themselves. It is therefore necessary that we should assist this enterprise; but the provisions made to carry it tc completion are altogether deficient. If you want to have this enterprise as a transcontinental railway from ocean to ocean, in course of time, at least from the Pacific ocean to the St. Lawrence, why is the method of carying out that project covered with these blemishes? Why did you not bring forward a project which would at once have made all these companies into one, and then deal with the project?
There are other serious considerations in this matter. We have been told that we are to have $40,000,000 of the stock of the



company. What is 'be the total stock of the.company? My right hon. friend has presented a view which is new to me, and which I cannot understand in the face of the resolution. To-day there is against these twenty-eight companies a stock issue of $158,000,000. Of this, $77,000,000 is the stock issue of the Canadian Northern, leaving $81,000,000 as the stock issue of the subsidiary companies. I cannot read that in the resolution; but if this stock issue is to be wiped out, which is something to which I would not object, what are you going to do as regards the $18,000,000 for which that stock is pledged? I desire an explanation of that. So far as I understand the matter, however, the stock of the subsidiary companies is to be wiped out, and	the	stock	of	the	CanadianNorthern railway is to be fixed at $100,000,000. The Canadian Northern covenants with the contractors that in consideration of the transfer of the shares of the capital stock mentioned in clause (a) of paragraph 2, hereof, it will by proper corporate action cause to be alloted to the contractors or their nominees fully paid and non-assessable shares of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern of the par valve of twenty-three million dollars being the difference between the present issued share capital of the Canadian Northern and the amount to which its capital is increased by the statute.

That the shares mentioned in the first part of the schedule shall be vested in the Canadian Northern, subject only to the charge tliereon created by and to the terms of the new trust deed.

This matter was discussed in the House before, and it was pointed out that one of the companies here mentioned, the Canadian Northern Pacific, had an agreement with the Government of British Columbia whereby the control of the tolls was expressly taken away from the Government of Canada and placed under the jurisdiction of the Government of British Columbia. When two years ago the Government succeeded in putting through the House a measure giving a subsidy to that branch of the road, we on this side contended that this road should not be subsidized or assisted because the company was under the control of the province of British Columbia, not only in respect of traffic originating in British Columbia, but in respect of traffic going into that province. The part of the contract with the province of British Columbia to which I allude is as follows:
In consideration of the guarantee of the securities hereunder, the Northern Company covenants that the Pacific Company will agree that the Lieutenant Governor in Council, may from time to time, having due regard in so doing to the position and interests of the Pacific Company, and In the case of traffic destined to or originating in the other provinces of Canada, bearing also in mind the desirability of obtaining reasonable rates from points in the province of British Columbia to points in the other provinces or vice versa, modify any rates established by the Pacific Company for the carriage of freight and passengers to and from all points on the said aided lines within the province of British Columbia, provided always, that before any rates are so modified, the Pacific Company shall be heard and its interests taken into consideration as aforesaid; provided further, that if the Pacific Company shall at nnv time

be dissatisfied with any rates so modified by the Lieutenant Governor in Council, it shall have the right to appeal from the order modifying any such rates, to the Supreme Court ot British Columbia. Any such appeal shall be heard before the chief justice and one of the justices, or before two of the justices of such court (thereafter referred to as the Appellate Tribunal) who, upon any notice of appeal being given, shall be nominated by the Lieutenant Governor in Council to hear and determine such appeal. The Appellate Tribunal, in the event of any such appeal, shall have authority, and it shall be its duty, to inquire into the whole matter, with power to call and examine on oath or otherwise such witness as either party may desire, to examine into, or cause to be examined into, all books, vouchers or accounts of the company, to call in the assistance of such experts, and generally to make such investigations as it may be deemed desirable to enable it to determine the matters involved in such appeal, and thereupon it may either confirm, modify, disallow, or revise such rates so appealed against. Any rates so modified or determined by the order of the Lieutenant Governor in Council, in conformity with the provisions of this section, shall, except as modified on such appeal, be rates which the Pacific Company will he entitled to enforce in respect of the services covered by such rates. The Canadian Northern railway undertakes that it will not and that the Pacific Company will agree that it will not bring or promote any appeal to the Railway Commission of Canada from any order made under and pursuant to the provisions of this section, and in the event of any such appeal being brought by others, that the Northern Company and the Pacific Company, will represent to the commission on such appeal, that it is satisfied with the rates the subject of such appeal, in so far as they are or have been established within the provisions of this section.
This agreement is standing to-day. It is very true that if this resolution passes into law the Railway Commission shall have jurisdiction over the rates in British Columbia, but subject to the provisions of the agreements. Why is this ?
Under what clause ?

Under this clause:
That they and each and every of them will from time to time enter into agreements with the Government for the mutual interchange of traffic between the Canadian Northern and the constituent companies or any of them, with the Government railways, and the terms and conditions of every such agreement shall he such as the parties thereto may agree upon or in default of agreement, as may be settled by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada (hereinafter called the ' Railway Board '), and the Railway Board shall have power from time to time upon the application of the Governor in Council or of any party to any such agreement to vary, modify or rescind the same provided always that every agreement respecting the interchange of traffic shall be subject to any agreements now existing with any other company or companies.
Will the right hon. gentleman tell me what that clause has to do with the control of rates ?

It has this to do with it: Each one of these companies is preserving its identity; therefore under this resolution they can arrange their rates as independent companies for the interchange of traffic. Each of these companies has its own rights, and these rights cannot be interfered with except by agreement; therefore every arrangement regarding interchange of traffic made between them must be subject to the existing agreement between the province of British Columbia and the Canadian Northern Pacific. Does my hon. friend pretend to say that if the legislation based upon this resolution becomes law I cannot send a car of freight from Montreal to British Columbia without its being liable to be detained at the British Columbia boundary line and being made subject to additional tolls by the' Canadian Northern Pacific Railway Company? If we had only one company, then the question of interchange of traffic would not arise, but, as it stated specifically here, we have all these companies, each preserving its own identity, and the Canadian Northern Pacific Company has the right to make its own tariff under its agreement, and that agreement is preserved and not subject to the supervision of the Railway Board. If that is not the effect of this contract, there is time yet to change it. Does my right hon. friend intend to alter this disposition ?

But 1 contend that when the Parliament of Canada, at the instigation of my right hon. friend, says that the Railway Commission shall have jurisdiction, but subject only to an existing agreement, my right hon. friend has ousted the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. I contend, on the contrary, that the Railway Commission has full jurisdiction, because my right hon. friend very wisely
provided that the Canadian Northern Pacific railway shall come under the jurisdiction of Canada, by being declared a work for the general advantage of Canada. But whilst my right hon. friend has claimed that we have jurisdiction over that railway through the Railway Commission, at the same time the agreement says: 'Subject, however, to the .agreement which has been made by the Canadian Northern Pacific Railway Company.5 Sir, this company never should have received a dollar of subsidy from this Gov-[DOT]ernment. We took that position two years ago; but the Prime Minister had the weakness to agree to a stipulation that would not permit even an appeal to be taken to the Railway Commission of Canada. To-day, whilst we give this bounty to this enterprise, and claim jurisdiction for the Railway Commission over the railway, we are very careful to say to the commission that we will exercise that jurisdiction only subject to the agreement which exists in reference to the Canadian Northern Pacific Company.
These are some of the objections which I have to urge. I said at the beginning that I had not the intention of going deeply into the subject; but I said that I would not fail to show the salient objections that we had to this agreement. Let me recapitulate. The first objection we have to this agreement is that although it purports to be a unification of the Canadian Northern system, it is no such unification-that the twenty-eight companies are still in existence, and will continue as they are to-day. The next point is that the guarantees that w7e have are absolutely illusory, that the mortgage which we receive is absolutely insufficient.
I said a moment ago, and I repeat, that this enterprise must go on. It has been conceived for the benefit of the Canadian people. We require this railway. My right hon. friend said he would not let it go into liquidation. It must not go into liquidation, but we should have the control of it. Since we must go into partnership with the Canadian Northern railway, let us see that we are the master, not the servant. Let the agreement be modified; let the resolutions be modified. But, sir, as they stand at the present time, they are not conceived for the benefit of the Canadian people; they are conceived altogether for the benefit of the firm of Mackenzie and Mann and of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Sir, we have no objection to helping them. We have helped them in the past. 1 for my part have been an admirer of their energy and enterprise. I have not much in common with them; I cannot claim them as friends;

but I admire energy, enterprise and pluck wherever it is found. At the same time, there is this consideration to be borne in mind by the Prime Minister, that there are interests which are transcendent, and the primary of those transcendent interests is that of the country. I have to repeat that the interest of the country is not served by the present resolutions, and as they stand it will become the duty of the Opposition to oppose them from first to last.

Mr. Speaker, it is one of many interesting features of the character of the right hon. the leader of the Opposition that one is never able to predicate with any certainty the position he will assume, and assume for his party, on any public question. Very little assistance can be gained by a review of his past attitude on similar questions, and usually very little assistance can be gained by a study of the afdvance notices offered by his followers in particular instances. In the case at present under review, we find that even the Toronto Globe is a very unsafe guide in prophesying the position of the Liberal leader. We had been led to expect by the thunder and fire we have heard and seen from the city of Toronto in the last two weeks-yes, in the last two months and a half-that the Liberal party was ready to set its face unalterably against any assistance to Mackenzie and Mann; that it was going to stand between the people of Canada and the dissipating of their resources. We have heard it said that the Government of the day had sold out the people of this country, and that there was to be no sham fight. Even before the proposals of the Government were known, the position of the Liberal party in this country, in antagonism to those proposals, was flourished throughout the world by a section of the Liberal press. However, when the day of battle comes, we find the Liberal leader not setting his face against assistance to the Canadian Northern, but taking exception to certain details of the Government's proposals, and admitting, after he takes all his exceptions, that he does not understand the proposals at all. I am disposed to agree with the Liberal leader in that latter statement. I am also disposed to congratulate him on having shown himself on this occasion the leader of his party, and that he has not allowed the

petulant malice of a Toronto editor to stampede and dragoon him into a wild and unreasoning opposition.
I said that the Liberal leader had admitted that he did not understand the resolutions now before the House. At the same time-as he finished his speech, and indeed at various times throughout his remarks-he emphasized that he was unalterably opposed to these resolutions, and that he was going to oppose them from beginning to end. If I might offer a word ' of advice it would be this: that the attitude of a party, as of an individual, toward any proposal had better be reserved until that party or individual thoroughly understands what the proposal is. I am free to admit that the resolutions before the House are not of the simplest imaginable character. The situation that presented itself for solution was not a simple situation; it was an exceedingly complicated and difficult situation, and it was found that the interests of the country coulid only be preserved by an arrangement that necessarily involved very many and very difficult intricacies. However, I believe-and I am more firmly convinced after listening to the right hon. leader of the Opposition-that the Government's proposals have in the end been reduced to as simple, compact, and thoroughgoing a form as it was possible to reduce them to.
The right hon. gentleman opened his speech with the statement that the alternative that presented itself to the Government of allowing the road to go into liquidation was an unthinkable alternative. Consequently, I need not address myself to a consideration of that alternative at all. The alternative, if it presented itself at all, of permitting the road to go into liquidation was unthinkable. The time for contemplation of that point has gone by. Likewise the hour for considering whether or not we shall go ahead with a third transcontinental system in this country has also gone by. That question is now properly eliminated from discussion. The seal of this country was put upon the third transcontinental system, indelibly and irrevocably, in 1911 by the late Liberal Government. The sanction of Canada was given by the Government headed by the present leader of the Opposition when he guaranteed the bonds of the great connecting link between Montreal and Port Arthur to the extent of $35,000,000. Whatever may be the merits of the question as to whether a third transcontinental system was necessary in Canada, those merits cannot now logically be taken under

36a3
review at all. The hour for discussion has gone by, and once the seal and endorsement of this country was affixed to those thirty-five millions of bonds for the connecting link, we were committed, and committed irrevocably, to the third transcontinental system. It may, however, be worth while to reflect at the present time that when that responsibility was assumed by the Government of the day in May, 1911, the question was brought before that Government in words of warning and in words of weight by the present Prime Minister as to whether or not the Government had assured themselves on sufficient information and data that it was advisable to encourage by the sanction of this country the completion of a third transcontinental system; I would respectfully refer hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House to the words of the leader of the Opposition of that day, the present Prime Minister, when he warned the Government that a very serious responsibility was being lightly undertaken-that even then the traffic over the one transcontinental was not sufficient to occupy more than about one-fifth of its capacity, and when he declared that it might well be that we were taking a false step in affixing the seal and endorsement of this country to that great issue of bonds. However, the time for meditation and reflection on that phase of the question has gone by. The country is committed to it whether it be a success or a failure, and we are bound in justice to its bond-holders, but far more so in justice to the people of this country, to see that transcontinental railway to completion. It is only just to say that in the conflict that may take place between the three rivals for the transcontinental traffic of this country, there are very important advantages that will accrue to the Canadian Northern in the contest; and there is every reason now to say that in the struggle that will ensue the Canadian Northern railway will not be the unfittest to survive. Many and great are its advantages over the Canadian Pacific railway itself, in some respects,, and more and greater still are its advantages over the Transcontinental railway as constructed by the late Government.
What, then, is the position of the Liberal party at the present time? The leader of the Opposition says:	We are committed to
it; failure or collapse is an unspeakable alternative. But, he says: I do not favour the present proposal, because the company does not come to us admitting that it is unable to pay its debts and that failure or collapse is the alternative if we do not
come to its assistance. Why, he says: there are some ten and a half million dollars of floating liabilities and the men who own the stock of the Canadian Northern come forward and agree in the terms of this Bill to themselves provide for the excess of these floating liabilities over the normal figure without recourse to the current securities, and that, he interprets as an admission that the company are not in extremis at all, but are quite able to take care of their own liabilities at the present time.
A word in the first place as to the general principle there laid down by the leader of the Opposition, and then I will have a word to say as to the premises on which he bases it. ' If ' he says, ' it appears to me that this company cannot get along without assistance I would do again as I did in 1911 and I would loan them the money to see them through.' In other words, if it appears to the leader of the Opposition that the Canadian Northern Railway Company were not at the present time able to carry on their enterprises without assistance, he would lend them the money out of the treasury of the country and he would take no compensation in return. On what security would he lend them the money? He says, our present security is illusory. Can he name anything possessed by the Canadian Northern or by the other companies that we do not take security on? Then, if it appeared to the leader of the Opposition that this company were in extremis and bound to ask for aid or default, he would lend the money, give them $45,000,000 on the same security we have taken or on less security, and he would undertake that liability and perform that service and take back not one dollar's worth of compensation from the company. There stands the Liberal party.
If I can convince the leader of the Opposition that the company does require this money and cannot succeed without it, then doubtless we will have the support of the Liberal party in this House and we will have the emphatic support of the leader of the Opposition, especially when he reflects that we are not guaranteeing the bonds for nothing but that we are getting two-fifths stock in the enterprise as a compensation therefor. The floating liability it is true, in so far as it exceeds at the present time the normal figure, must be taken care of aside from the guaranteed securities and their proceeds, within one year. It must be reduced to the normal figure within that time and in the meantime they must be pro-
