tected against action. But what does that mean? It means that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, the contractors, under subsection (b) of section 4 of the Bill, are bound themselves to see to it that the floating or current liability of the Canadian Northern is reduced within one year to three million dollars, or to such normal amount as the Government may decide to be correct, and that that must be done without recourse to the proceeds of the guaranteed security.
It will be asked, if they are able to do that, then what other liability is it they are not able to take care of? As the hon. gentleman knows, at the present time there stands on the construction account of the Canadian Northern a further liability, owing at the date of the audit, amounting to $21,262,000, entirely aside from the current indebtedness. This $21,262,000 has already been spent on construction, and is planted in the road to-day, and the Canadian Northern Railway Company owes that indebtedness to the men who did their work and supplied the material, and that indebtedness they are not in a position to meet. Why, says the leader of the Opposition, the temporary loans are taken care of. Very true. Twenty million dollars of temporary loans are protected at the present time by isome twenty-four million dollars of securities, and it is provided by the Bill that satisfactory covenants must be given that these securities, and these alone, will be resorted to - in order to satisfy the loans they have advanced. That takes care of temporary loans and floating liabilities, which must be taken care of, but what about the $21,262,000 that is owing on 'construction account? Would the right hon. gentleman tell me now how he would have that provided for by the Canadian Northern Railway Cbmpany? We have thrown everything on the table; he has access to every one of their assets, and to all their available securities, and he cannot point where the Canadian Northern Railway Company can go and discharge that liability of $21,262,000. The financial stringency that has overrun the world, as well as the increased cost of construction, has brought about such conditions that the Canadian Northern Railway Company at the present time faces a situation that it is not able to surmount without the assistance of this Government.
While I am at that point, it may be asked: How are Mackenzie, Mann and 
Company, Limited, going to reduce this sum of floating indebtedness to-the normal figure? My information, and the result of the investigation is this: that the Canadian Northern Railway Company has been under the necessity of providing out of its current revenues large sums in payment of instalments due on what is called 'equipment trust', and as	a consequence
the regular current indebtedness of the Canadian	Northern has
swollen away beyond the normal figure. The payments on equipment trust are payments made on the purchase of equipment. These payments are logically and correctly chargeable to capital, but the company was under the necessity of meeting them when they fell due and they met them out of current revenue. When that necessity is removed, as it will be removed by the present financial arrangement, then the company will be in a position to declare that they are quite capable of taking care of this excess of floating indebtedness over the normal figure, and to reduce it within a reasonable time to the normal figure.
As to temporary loans, very little need be said. It will be clear to all that with the rehabilitation of their credit that naturally results from the present arrangement, the securities that are pledged against these current loans will be amply sufficient and much more in all probability to take care of all liability thereon.
But the fact remains that the system at present stands in a position where it cannot, in the nature of things, be made a paying investment, be made to turn the way of success and away from the road to failure, unless funds are provided to take care of the completion of that road. What does it consist of: The Canadian Northern Pacific, the western lines between Port Arthur and the coast; a portion of the Canadian Northern Ontario uncompleted between Montreal and Port Arthur; other portions uncompleted in the province of Quebec; other large portions uncompleted in British Columbia which ought to, when completed, bring the road into contact with our western harbours. So long as it remains in the present condition it will not appeal to any business man that the road could possibly be a success as a road, but must proceed on the down grade and not on the highway to success. Consequently the road is in danger of failure at the present time. The situation is such that, through no fault of its own, so far as we are aware, the Canadian Northern

Railway Company is brought face to face with a situation where an arm stronger than its own must be extended, and where the assistance of the Government must come to it, or the Canadian Northern railway cannot be anything but a failure. That being the case, the right hon. the leader of the Opposition is bound to reverse his party position and come to the assistance of the Government and help to put through these resolutions which provide for the guarantee, that he -would give for nothing, being given in return for a two-fifths proprietorship of the road.
A further objection taken by the leader of the Opposition is that we have not reduced the capitalization. After all, he says, we have only pretended to reduce the capitalization. That is what I understand to be the point he makes. Under the plan that the leader of the Opposition would follow, he would not make even a pretence. If he" believed that the road needed the money and had to have it, he would lend it just as he did in 1911, and he would not even go through the formality of reducing the capitalization at all. But we have reduced the capitalization; and I think I shall be able to convince him on this point, that he was quite correct when he made the statement that he did not understand the resolutions. What do the resolutions say? They say that, before any guarantee is given, all these allied companies must have their various stocks passed to the trustee as security, the beneficial interest subject to that mortgage being in the Canadian Northern road; that is to say, the Canadian Northern road must be'come the absolute owners, subject to this mortgage which protects the Government, of all the stock of the eighteen companies at present owned by Mackenzie and Mann. There are eleven other companies at present owned by the Canadian Northern itself, their stocks and bonds being already pledged to secure the perpetual debentures issue of 1903; but 18 companies have almost their total stock issue clear in the name of Mackenzie and Mann, Limited. These companies have to put their stock in the Canadian Northern, impressing it first with a charge for the protection of this guarantee. My right hon. friend says: You put those stocks in, you put $25,000,000 of the stock of the Canadian Northern Ontario; you put in twenty-five millions dollars of the stock of the Canadian Northern Padific; you put the stock of the Central Ontario; you put the stock of the Canadian Northern Quebec; you put the stock, six millions dollars or
almost that, of the Quebec and lake St. John and after you have put them all into the Canadian Northern, those stocks still exist. It is quite true that they do exist. No one says that these stocks are burned or wiped out. They exist, but none the less the capitalization is reduced to the capital of the company that owns these stocks and all the assets of these companies.
Oh, oh.

The right hon. gentleman laughs. What is the purpose of a reduction of capitalization? How is the public interested in that reduction? Because, if a public utility is over capitalized and the stock gets into the hands of the public, that is a lever in the hands of the public giving them a right to a revenue on that stock and consequently a lever for the upkeep of freight rates; but if you take that stock and keep it out of the hands of the public, put it where it never can possibly get into the hands of the public, and make it owned by the Canadian Northern railway, whose capitalization is reduced to $100,000,000, how possibly can you have any further evil result from overcapitalization? You have idone everything that possibly can be done to prevent every ill that ever comes from over-capitalization. The companies still exist in any case; but the stock belongs to the Canadian Northern railway; all the profits of those companies go to the Canadian Northern railway, and the Canadian Northern railway is capitalized at $100,000,000 and no more. Consequently $100,000,000 and no more is the stock which has any right to earn dividends. That must be clear to my right hon. friend, and I feel quite certain that he understands it just as well as I do. The capitalization, in so far as it is a lever or can be used as an argument to affect freight rates or to affect the public in any way whatever, is reduced to $100,000,000. And we are the guardians of the public and of no one else.
Then my right hon. friend says: Why, that only applies anyway to the eighteen companies that Mackenzie and Mann own clear. They own the stock of those companies clear, each company of course being subject to its bonded indebtedness. But, he says, there are some other properties of which they do not own the stock, and the stock of which is already pledged. That is true. We get a first mortgage on the stocks that come into the Canadian Northern, in so far as they come in clear. In so far as the eighteen companies are con-

possibly be a success as a road, but must Mann, Limited, our mortgage comes upon the stock of these companies direct, a mortgage physically fixed on the stock of these eighteen companies. That is one constituent of the mortgage premises. That constitutes a real mortgage and forms the first constituent of the mortgage premises.
What comes next? The equity of the Canadian Northern railway in the eleven companies, the bonds and stock both, are already brought under the trust deed of 1903. In 1903, the bonds of the Canadian Northern Express Company, $3,000,000, the bonds of the Winnipeg Land Company and the stock of both companies, the bonds and stock of the Lake Superior Terminals, the bonds and stock of the Canadian Northern System Terminals, owning their terminals from shore to shore, all became at the time the bonds of the Canadian Northern, and were put in along with the Canadian Northern assets as security for the 4 per cent perpetual bond issue of 1903. Consequently the Canadian Northern own all these companies, both the bonded indebtedness and the stock issues, sulbject only to the charge created by that trust deed or mortgage of 1903. They hold the equity of redemption therein, and a laTge equity it is. We have taken care, in these resolutions and in the Bill which will follow it, to take that equity and place it as constituent No. 2 under the mortgage which we take to secure this guarantee. Was it not worth while taking it? In that way we take everything these companies have and, we place it under our mortgage as our security against our guarantee. Who is there who can suggest anything more that we can do? Would the hon. gentleman have us legislate the bonds out of existence in order that we could get a first charge? Would he legislate the priority out of existence for the benefit of the people of this country? Would he have confiscatory legislation? We have done everything we can to get the mortgage right down on all the assets left of all the companies that are there. Those assets are tremendous assets.
Furthermore, we take a physical mortgage on the Canadian Northern properties themselves. The Canadian Northern railway, operating the main line and all the 'branches between Port Arthur and Edmonton, about 5,350 miles, is able to give a mortgage on those assets alone. It cannot give a .mortgage on the assets of other companies; it

can give a mortgage on them only to the extent and in the form in which those assets come to it. But on its own physical road between Port Arthur, and Edmonton, the Canadian Northern gives a mortgage direct to the trustee for the protection of the guarantee of this country. Now, the hon. gentleman says:	Oh, this mortgage
is entirely illusory mortgage, because he says, there is indebtedness ahead of it. And in that he has the wonderful consolation of having the imprimatur of the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), who says ' hear, hear ' to the statement that ' the mortgage is entirely illusory.' Let me draw his attention to a number of these securities-and I know he is listening, though he affects not to be. The Canadian Northern railway itself has a road between Port Arthur and Edmonton which, with branches represents about 5,350 miles of railway. It owns its terminals and various other assets there; it owns its lands. Now, that road is already mortgaged, it is true; it has several bond issues against it. But it is the most valuable portion of the whole Canadian Northern system that is to be; it is the portion that has been paying and paying well, it is the portion that serves, if not the best, almost the best parts of the whole northwest country.
That is the portion which above all things must be preserved; it is the valuable asset of the Canadian Northern railway. Now, as I have said, that road is bonded already. But I ask the right hon. gentleman if he would not, dollar for dollar and mile for mile, rather have a mortgage on that road than on the Canadian Northern Ontario running through a wilderness which has no local traffic, or very little? I ask the right hon. gentleman again, which is the better security-the Canadian Northern Ontario running through a wilderness, a connecting link, or the western line of the Canadian Northern Railway system? I know that he would chouse the western road. Now, I tell him if he took all the securities which this 5,350 miles of railway are liable for and added to them this $45,000,000 he would still have the road charged at about the same figure per mile that he charged, to secure this country, on the Canadian Northern Ontario. He took a mortgage, to secure the guarantee of the people of Canada on the Canadian Northern Ontario, at the rate of $35,000 per mile-he took a first mortgage, it is true, on most of it, or in effect a first mortgage. And if he adds the whole $45,000,000 to the present indebtedness of the

Canadian Northern Railway western line, he would only reach the charge of practically $35,000 a mile. So, if one security is ' illusory '-even assuming that we have nothing else than the physical road of the Canadian Northern railway on the western plains-what is to be said of the security he took in 1911?-and got no compensation. But further, does the right hon. gentleman realize what security he did get in 1911? He just took a mortgage on the rails, the right of way, and, I suppose, the stations. He did not provide for a mortgage on the floating assets and current revenues of the company. But we have provided for it in this case, for if the company goes into liquidation our mortgage takes effect on everything it is fastened to now, and immediately fastens itself on the floating assets of the company and all its cash, revenues, etc. What does the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) think of his Government that brought down a Bill to this Parliament to guarantee the bonds of the Canadian Northern Ontario for $35,000,000 and did not take a dollar of compensation for this country or a dollar's worth of stock, and only took security on the rails, the right of way and the stations-on the mere road itself-did not even have the terminals? So, if we took over the road all we should have would be a bare railway, without a terminal, without a connection, without a traffic arrangement, without anything else.
But we do not stop there. We have already three constituent elements in our security. We have the stocks of eighteen companies- the stocks clear of incumbrance-we have the stocks and bonds of eleven more companies subject to the mortgage of 1903, and we have a mortgage on the Canadian Northern Railway western lines subject to the mortgages on the physical lines and properties themselves. But we have more than that, we have a mortgage on the whole town-site properties of Mackenzie, Mann, Limited. That is a portion of the resolution which the right hon. gentleman may have understood, but I notice that he said nothing about it. What does it mean? The Canadian Northern Railway Company are not the owners of these townsites, they made no investment in these townsites; the moneys were all laid out by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. Lands were sold them by this Government, paid for by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, and they purchased lands at various points as well. The expenditures have been made by them and by them alone, and'these lands belong to them, they are legally their
possession, just as the land of any owner is his possession. There is a charge against these townsites in this way:	The lands
which the right hon. Prime Minister referred to, some 4,100,000 acres, belonged to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited as their property. That is to say, that the Canadian Northern itself, owning the stock of all the other companies, or any one of the others, as the Canadian Northern Pacific, will, if called upon at any time, enter into an agreement for the mutual interchange of traffic with a Government railway. The terms they are to agree upon mutually. If they cannot agree, the Board of Railway

Commissioners is empowered to fix the terms, but no terms can be fixed affecting this traffic arrangement between the individual company and the Government railway that nullifies any agreement already entered into. In the first place, if this clause is never acted upon, there is no repeal of the general clause establishing jurisdiction, is there? If we never call upon the Canadian Northern Pacific to make a traffic arrangement with a Government railway, then the clause is never acted upon, and consequently there is no repeal, even if there were a repeal, if it were acted upon. I pause for any objection, if there is any objection to the reasoning so far. There is no objection, and consequently that is quite clear. Then, who in the world can conceive of the Government, owning the Intercolonial railway, calling upon the Canadian Northern Pacific 2,000 miles away, to enter into a traffic arrangement? The -Canadian Northern Pacific is confined to the province of British Columbia, and how in the world can it make a traffic arrangement with the Intercolonial railway that never gets west of the province of Quebec? Consequently the point raised by my right hon. friend, to say the most of it, is a purely academic one. There is no conceivable possibility of a traffic arrangement between any constituent company in British Company and any Government railway, is there?
I go farther. Not only wiill the clause never be acted upon, so far as anyone can see, with regard to the Canadian Northern Pacific; but if it were acted upon, it would not have the effect for one minute of impairing in the slightest degree the control of the Railway Commission as to rates. Let us say that the Government owns a railway that runs to British Columbia, and it says to the Canadian Northern Pacific in British Columbia: We want to make a traffic arrangement with you for the interchange of traffic? What is a traffic arrangement? It is an arrangement for the interchange of traffic and for the apportionment of rates. Well, suppose we have a line running to British Columbia, and the Canadian Northern Pacific railway is asked to make an arrangement with us for the interchange of traffic and the apportionment of rates between us. If we cannot agree, the Railway Commission decides how the traffic is to be interchanged and how the rates are to be apportioned. Now, how in the world can that ever interfere in any way whatever with any agreement 2334
between the Canadian Northern Pacific and the British Columbia Government as to control of rates? It does not matter what the rates are. All the traffic [DOT] arrangement does is to apportion the rates, whatever they may be, and to agree upon an arrangement by which traffic shall -be interchanged. The rates are fixed by the Railway Commission. The apportionment of them is fixed by the traffic arrangement.
Furthermore, the agreement that the right hon. gentleman has referred to between the Canadian Northern Pacific and the British Columbia Government is not a traffic arrangement at all. Therefore, for a third reason it can not possibly interfere with the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission, because the meaning of that clause would be, and it was intended to be and is, that, while if there is any traffic arrangement such as that we have, as a Government, "with another road, that traffic arrangement Shall not he violated by any terms the Railway Commission shall make. As a matter of fact we have a traffic arrangement. I am informed that the Canadian Northern has no traffic arrangement with any company, but the Government of this country has a traffic arrangement with the Grand Trunk, made by the right hon. gentleman himself, for the interchange -of traffic at the city of Montreal. As a consequence, we were bound to protect the country by saying that we could not be called upon to make a traffic arrangement with the Canadian Northern that would be a violation of our obligations under our traffic arrangement with the Grand Trunk. That is the effect of clause (b), of which the right hon. gentleman is so much afraid.
I recapitulate as follows the reasons why there is nothing in the objection of my right hon. friend. First, there is no conceivable possibility of the clause being acted upon with regard to the Canadian Northern Pacific at all, because we have no line that connects that can make a traffic arrangement with it. Second, if there were a traffic arrangement between any two companies, it could be made apportioning the rates between them without in any way violating any arrangement with any Government as to the rates themselves. Third, the agreement made by the Canadian Northern Pacific with the Government of British Columbia is not a traffic arrangement at all.
I think I have passed in review, perhaps not fully, but as fully as the time at my

disposal will permit, all tlie objections raised by the right hon. leader of the Opposition to the resolutions of the Government.
I do not feel that I should be justified in delaying the House longer with a more detailed examination of the various provisions of the Bill. That can be better attended to in committee. While we believe this Bill to be complete, while we 'believe that it safeguards the public interest in every way, yet it is laid before the House not as an invulnerable document, not as an infallible document beyond all possibility of improvement, but as the proposal of the Government to which we invite criticism from hon. gentlemen opposite as well as from hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. And if the Bill can be improved in the public interest, it is open for improvement, and we will welcome any suggestions along that line. But, Sir, we lay the Bill on the table of the House and before this Parliament as the solution proposed by us of a very vast and very difficult problem, a problem freighted with difficulties on every side; and we say, in laying it before this Parliament, that we believe it at once preserves the public interest and does justice to all the fair claims of private capital; for only by concurrent regard for the rights ol private enterprise and the promotion of the public welfare can the ultimate ends of government be properly subserved.

If my
intention in rising had been to reply to the hon. the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), his eloquent, able and comprehensive speech might, at the last moment, have deterred me. But, Sir, I have not risen with that intention. I have a conscious sense of embarrassment in rising to-night to express to this House and to the country the reason for my differing with iny party on this measure. It is not a pleasant thing to differ from men who have been one's confreres for a length of time, and it is an accentuated unpleasantness where the position one takes is seized upon by the representatives of the opposite party and his conclusions and his motives distorted.
When I accepted the nomination for the city of Kingston I reserved to myself the right to exercise my judgment and express my views on such subjects as were not fundamental to the Conservative party, and it is in the exercise of that right that I rise to my feet this evening. Sir, I do not be-

lieve that there is a man in this House tonight who is more loyal to the principles of the Conservative party as he understands them than am I. But I am not willing to admit that it is necessary to the solidarity of party government that the crack of the party whip should be so loud and its sting so sharp that individual responsibility shouild be absolutely abrogated.
I have, as I say, some difficulty in approaching this subject. My good friend the Solicitor General has frankly admitted that the Government places this Bill on the table not wedded to its terms, that they are prepared to have it discussed and to accept amendments if in their opinion they are such as should be adopted.
It is a strange thing what >an important part railway legislation has played in the history of this country. In the fifties we had the Grand Trunk Railway Company; in the sixties we had the Intercolonial railway; in the seventies and early eighties we had the Canadian Pacific railway; at the end of the century we had the minor Ontario railways and the proposed railway in the Yukon; and from 1900 we have had the National Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern railway. In my judgment there is much of truth in what the Solicitor General has said in his criticism of the construction of the National Transcontinental railway and as to the effect of that road a.$ a competing road for the lessening of rates. If I understand the principle which underlay the construction of that road it is that Mr. Hays thought that the increased cost of railway operation through the increase of wages and prices of material, necessitated the construction of a road which would permit of long trains being economically drawn. But when the cost of the Transcontinental was so augmented, through irregularities and extravagance that the interest charges became excessive, then, I say, the National Transcontinental ceased to be a factor in competitive railway rates in this country. If I understand correctly the attitude of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, or the Canadian Northern Railway Company, they approached the problem from an altogether different point of view. Their road was constructed more .after the manner of a colonization road. The original cost of construction was reduced to a minimum with the idea of improving the road iut of earnings or improving it indirectly as money might be available. And it follows necessarily,

where grades are high and curves are sharp, that the cost of operation must be high although the expenditure for construction is small and the interest charges comparatively low. I do not know that any opinion of mine as to what would have been the wise thing for the Liberal party to have done in 1903 will carry the slightest weight or be deemed worthy of attention. But I submit for the consideration of this House 'and the country at large, that from the point of view of economy-and I want to emphasize that word, ' economy '-it would have been better for the Government of that day to have made some arrangement with the then existing transcontinental road the Canadian Pacific railway, around the head of lake Superior, than have put Canada to the expense of building another road there. But there is another consideration besides that of economy. I do not know the motives that actuated the present leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). It may be that he was inspired with the idea that Canada through the West should be something more than a line, that it should have breadth as well as length, and that he felt that from a national and political point of view it was well that Canada should be broadened around the head of lake Superior, and therefore favoured the construction of the second transcontinental railway. However, Sir, when We come to the question of 1911, it has always puzzled me why the then Minister of Railways and Canals promoted the construction of a third transcontinental road by guarantee of $35,000 per mile of some 1,000 miles of road. Surely it would have been the wiser plan to have incorporated the National Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern Railway system into one road. It would have been more ^economical land certainly it would have served equally well the national and political outlook. But that plan was not adopted, and I suppose that but little is to be gained by looking into the past rather than into the future. But before I leave the past, I would like to direct the attention of this House and of the country at large, and more particularly of my constituents, to the fact that when last year application was made to the Government for further'assistance to the Canadian Northern Railway Company, I was outspoken within my own party in stating my objections to any aid being granted without a full and ample inquiry.
I told those then in authority that in my judgment the amount required would never
complete the Canadian Northern Railway system. I was, however, confronted with the statement then made by an official of the Canadian Northern railway that if that money were granted that railway system would be enabled to carry its work to completion. I was told that to stop that work would be a national calamity; that the Canadian Northern railway was so closely allied with the financial interests of this country that if the work were stopped, financial chaos would result and Canada would suffer a setback from which she could not recover for half a century. Possibly I was wrong in yielding to that argument without full examination, but, as you will remember, Sir, the Bill was brought down to the House in the dying hours of the session and there was little opportunity for inquiry and investigation. This year, however, when the matter came first to the attention of the House, through an insidious and persistent lobby that was carried on by the Canadian Northern interests, it seemed to me that the time had come for a thorough examination and inquiry into the development and organization and relation to the Government of the Canadian Northern Railway system. After giving that matter the most careful consideration that I have been able to give it, permit me, Sir, to-say that I am of the opinion to-night that I held a year ago; that it was a mistake in 1913 to have assisted the Canadian Northern railway, and that the bargain that the Government suggests to-day is a bad bargain for the Dominion of Canada.
I want to look back a little into the history of the Canadian Northern railway. I should like this country to understand just how this undertaking has been organized and managed. I do not know whether members of this House know the history of this company, but I do know that it took me many weary hours to worm out from the statutes of this country the financial wanderings of this road, and the intricacies of its amalgamation and absorbing corporations. I want this House to come back with me to the year 1880, when certain gentlemen presented a petition to this House asking for an incorporation for the Nelson Valley Railway and Transportation Company. The prayer of the petition had the favourable ear of the House and by 43 Victoria, chapter 57, authority was granted to that railway to undertake certain operations, and by 43 Victoria, chapter 59, similar powers were granted to the Winnipeg and Hudson's Bay Railway and Steamship Company. The Nelson Valley Company had power to build a rail-

land, and by an arrangement entered into with the Manitoba Government-and my right hon. friend the leader of the Government this afternoon when directing attention to the fact that these charters of the Winnipeg company and the Manitoba company were for years peddled around without a purchaser failed to direct the attention of the House to the radical change that took place when Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann bought this charter. Up to the time they got their grant of $8,000 per mile from the Manitoba Government, all these companies had was the land grant and the transport subsidy, with an assurance that certainly merited recognition from the point of view of railway financing, they had the courage to make application to the Manitoba Government for a guarantee of $8,000 per mile to build a road that they had admitted could be built for $11,700 per mile. That shows that the Dominion of Canada is behind this undertaking to the extent of $280,209,765. What has this company done for Canada ? I have heard considerable to-night from the Solicitor General, who, with that eloquence that always characterizes his utterances and with that effectiveness of speaking that at times stamps a fallacious argument as being effective, made the statement that the Canadian Northern Railway Company was a competitive railroad and that it would lower or regulate rates. If I have not quoted him correctly or given the spirit of his language, I would like him to correct me. I understood him to say that while the National Transcontinental railroad would never be a regulating factor owing to the cost of construction, the Canadian Northern Railway Company would be. I want to take him on his own statement, and I want to quote, in reply to him, not what the Canadian Northern Company say when they want further assistance from the Government, but what they said when they wanted to keep up freight rates. I want to

quote what the Hon. Mr. Phippen argued before the Railway Commission on the Consolidated Western Freight Rates Case. All of the evidence and ninety-nine per cent of the argument has been directed against the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. We have hardly heard the name of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company mentioned, we have hardly heard the name of the Canadian Northern Railway Company mentioned by the Complainants. It has been avoided by them as a thing accursed. Their whole case is built up,, with the exception of some statements which Mr. Pitblado made, and which I will deal with later, upon conditions which exist on the Canadian Pacific railway. The expert brought by the Government, Mr. Muller, says that the Canadian Pacific railway should be the road upon which these rates should be based, and the rates upon which the Canadian Northern should be compelled to carry its traffic.
He says further, that in determining what are-reasonable rates for the Canadian Pacific railway this board should not take into consideration any benefits which were given to the Canadian! Pacific Railway Company under its agreement with the Government, except perhaps the land grant of twenty five million acres. He says that the Canadian Northern railway, constructed at a time when, putting it moderately, it took $3 to get the same result as $1 would bring when the Canadian Pacific was constructed, should be compelled to compete with, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, not only upon the basis of the Canadian Pacific turning over to the public the benefit of all the advantages which were given to it under the terms of its contract, but turning over also to the public the benefit of the increased value of the dollar which went into the road, in other words, the unearned increment of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company between the time when that road was constructed in 1881, and the heyday of prosperity when the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railways were built.
Now, let us see a little more minutely just what that would mean. Let us take the Canadian Northern beginning at Port Arthur and follow it west, and as we go let us apply Mr. Muller's theory to the conditions with which, he would have us compete. We start at Port Arthur and we build to the Red river through probably as expensive a bit of country to construct a road in as there is in Canada. We build that line at the request both of the Government of the province of Manitoba and the Government of the province of Ontario, and we build the line necessarily alongside the line of the Canadian Pacific railway at the request of these provinces as a competitive line to meet Canadian Pacific railway conditions. What would Mr. Muller make conditions under which he would have us compete? The Government of the Dominion of Canada built the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and presented it to the company unden the terms of the agreement of 1881 ; The Canadian Northern railway built the line w'hich it operates out of its own

money, raised on its own bonds, guaranteed, if you will, by the province of Manitoba, but bonds for which it primarily and the people of the province of Manitoba secondarily are responsible. Mr. Muller would say that we must compete with the Canadian Pacific railway line which was presented to it on the basis of there "being no capital charge for the construction of our line.
